pages.title: Transit API
pages.description: Documentation for the Detroit Automation Academy's live transit data: DDOT and QLINE vehicle positions and DDOT service alerts as static JSON, plus the logged history dataset.
headings: Example response (real response, 2026-10-15; trimmed to 1 of 4 vehicles)
pages.text: Transit API — Detroit Automation Academy Developer documentation The transit API. This is the live data feed behind the academy’s Live Transit map and the bus count on the Live Transit page : Detroit Department of Transportation (DDOT) bus positions, QLINE streetcar positions, and DDOT service alerts, published as static JSON files on this site. A GitHub Actions workflow in the academy’s site repository rebuilds the files from the agency feeds about every 5 minutes. No key required. Base URL: https://detroitautomationacademy.com Endpoints GET /live-data/vehicles.json Parameters None. Refresh The build workflow runs about every 5 minutes and republishes the file when the underlying data has changed (and at least every 30 minutes as a liveness heartbeat). GitHub Pages may serve a cached copy for up to 10 minutes. Judge freshness by generated_at , never by fetch time. CORS Served by GitHub Pages with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * — call it directly from browser JavaScript. Auth None to read. The upstream DDOT key is a secret of the build workflow and never appears in the published files. Example response (real response, 2026-10-15; trimmed to 1 of 4 vehicles) { "generated_at": "2026-10-16T00:00:29.484Z", "count": 4, "vehicles": [ { "agency": "qline", "route_id": "QLINE", "vehicle_id": "287", "lat": 42.33913040161133, "lon": -83.05245971679688, "bearing": 154, "speed_mph": null, "updated_at": "2026-10-15T23:59:59.000Z" } ], "sources": { "ddot": { "ok": true, "at": "2026-10-16T00:00:29.484Z", "vehicles": 0, "batches_ok": 4, "batches_failed": 0 }, "smart": { "ok": true, "at": "2026-10-16T00:00:29.484Z", "vehicles": 141 }, "qline": { "ok": true, "at": "2026-10-16T00:00:29.484Z", "vehicles": 4 } } } Top-level fields Field Type Description generated_at string ISO 8601 UTC timestamp of when the build workflow generated this file. The file is only republished when the data changes (30-minute heartbeat aside), so this is the freshness clock for everything in it. count integer Number of vehicle objects in vehicles . vehicles array Live vehicle snapshots (fields below). sources object Per-agency feed status, keyed ddot , smart , qline : ok , at , and either vehicles (a count) or a reason . Two states are named explicitly: sources.ddot carries "configured": false with a reason when the build workflow lacks the upstream DDOT key — DDOT vehicles are then absent while other agencies still publish; sources.smart reports the status of the SMART display leg built from the Swiftly GTFS-Realtime feed: SMART vehicle positions are displayed in the Live Transit Detroit application only and are never part of this file's vehicles array or of the public JSON contract — the vehicles count under sources.smart counts positions published to the application's display payload, not records in this file. Vehicle fields Field Type Description agency string ddot or qline . route_id string GTFS route id: the route number for DDOT vehicles (the build covers all 37 DDOT routes), or QLINE for the streetcar. vehicle_id string Agency vehicle number. lat / lon number WGS84 position in decimal degrees. bearing number Compass heading in degrees, or null when the feed does not report it. speed_mph number Reported speed in miles per hour, or null when the feed does not report it. destination string DDOT records only: the destination text reported by the BusTime feed, or null . QLINE records do not carry this field. updated_at string Vehicle timestamp as reported by the agency feed (ISO 8601; DDOT timestamps are agency-local time without an offset). null when the feed reports none. GET /live-data/alerts.json Parameters None. Refresh Rebuilt on the same schedule as vehicles.json : about every 5 minutes when the alert set or a source state changes, with the same 30-minute heartbeat. CORS Served by GitHub Pages with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * . Auth None to read. Example response (real response, 2026-10-15) { "generated_at": "2026-10-15T19:51:06.386Z", "count": 0, "alerts": [], "sources": [ { "agency": "ddot", "kind": "realtime", "via": "bustime", "fetched_at": "2026-10-15T19:51:06.386Z", "ok": false, "status": "error", "alerts": 0, "reason": "DDOT_BUSTIME_KEY secret not configured", "configured": false } ] } Alerts top-level fields Field Type Description generated_at string ISO 8601 UTC timestamp of when the build workflow generated this file. count integer Number of alert objects in alerts . alerts array Active DDOT service bulletins (fields below). sources array Per-agency feed status as an array (in vehicles.json it is an object). Each entry carries agency , kind , via , fetched_at , ok , status ( ok or error ), and alerts (a count); a failed or unconfigured source adds a reason , and the not-configured state adds "configured": false . Bulletin fields Field Type Description id string Bulletin id from the BusTime feed. agency string ddot . header string Bulletin headline. description string Bulletin detail text. effect / cause string Currently always null — the BusTime bulletin feed does not carry GTFS-RT effect/cause values. active_period object {start, end} : start is the bulletin timestamp reported by the BusTime feed (agency-local ISO 8601, or null ); end is currently always null . routes / stops array Route ids and stop ids the bulletin applies to. url string Currently always null . source string bustime . fetched_at string When the build fetched this bulletin (the file’s generated_at ). kind string realtime . Retired endpoints The live data used to be served by a proxy at forge-line-live-proxy.netlify.app . Those endpoints were retired on 2026-10-15 — the proxy’s hosting quota was exhausted (it returned HTTP 503 usage_exceeded on every path) and the feed moved to the static files above. Do not build against them: GET https://forge-line-live-proxy.netlify.app/api/vehicles — retired 2026-10-15; use /live-data/vehicles.json instead. GET https://forge-line-live-proxy.netlify.app/api/alerts — retired 2026-10-15; use /live-data/alerts.json instead. GET https://forge-line-live-proxy.netlify.app/healthz — retired 2026-10-15; the static files need no health endpoint — check generated_at . Rate-limit etiquette Poll at most once per minute . The academy’s own map polls the vehicles file every 60 seconds — matching that is plenty. The files are rebuilt about every 5 minutes, so faster polling returns the same file; use generated_at to detect genuinely new data instead of re-polling. Cache responses client-side. Don’t fan out one page view into many parallel requests. The published files are the whole interface — there is no key to ask for and nothing upstream to bypass; the agency key exists only inside the build workflow. Building a student project or a community tool? The 5-minute cadence is the intended use. If you need something the feed doesn’t offer, the logged history below may already have it. Logged history dataset A public log of this feed’s snapshots, appended every 5 minutes, runs from 2026-10-03 — the raw material for headway analysis, reliability scores, and arrival predictions. Vehicle objects in the log use exactly the same field names as the live endpoint above, so code written against the live feed reads the history without translation. Repository: github.com/smit4786/forge-line-transit-data Format: forge-line.telemetry/v1 , documented in the repo’s SCHEMA.md Day index: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/smit4786/forge-line-transit-data/main/data/index.json One day of polls: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/smit4786/forge-line-transit-data/main/data/2026-10-03.jsonl (replace the date) Failed polls are never logged as empty records — a gap in a day’s file means that poll failed, not that zero buses were running. Error behavior Old generated_at — the files are static, so a failed or delayed build leaves the previous file in place rather than returning an error. If generated_at is well past the ~5-minute build cadence, treat the contents as of that timestamp and keep retrying on your normal cadence. A source reports "ok": false — that agency’s leg failed or is not configured (its reason says which); the other agencies’ data still publishes. Check sources before concluding the whole feed is down. Non-200 or network failure — back off and retry after 60 seconds. Don’t hammer the files; they only change every few minutes anyway. Empty vehicles array — valid response, no vehicles currently reporting on the covered routes (common late at night). File-level timestamps ( generated_at , fetched_at ) are UTC; vehicle and bulletin timestamps are reported as the agency feeds give them. Route coverage may expand as feeds are added; check sources to see which agencies are live. Attribution Built by Detroit Automation Academy. Live vehicle data: DDOT via Clever Devices BusTime; QLINE via its public GTFS-RT feed. Route shapes and stops: DDOT and QLINE GTFS. This feed is a community resource, published from the academy’s own repository — please follow the rate-limit etiquette above so it stays fast for everyone.

pages.title: Postmortem: Activating Empirical Timetable Substitution — Live Transit Detroit
pages.description: A postmortem on Phase 2b-ii of the Forge Line live transit layer: reported active, found inert, misdiagnosed twice, root-caused to a page-index/GTFS-ID translation gap, and verified with 18,002 substitutions.
pages.text: Postmortem: Activating Empirical Timetable Substitution — Live Transit Detroit · Detroit Automation Academy Live Transit Detroit · Installment 01 · October 2026 Postmortem: Activating Empirical Timetable Substitution Published October 6, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith Phase 2b-ii of the Forge Line live transit layer replaces scheduled bus segment times with measured typical times, once enough observations exist. It was reported active on October 5, found completely inert on October 6, misdiagnosed twice, and finally root-caused and activated the same day. This is the record. Summary The timetable stores stops as page indices into ddot-routes-3d.json ; timing cells are keyed by GTFS stop_id . The client looked up cells with page indices, so all 154 mature cells missed on every query. One translation function ( ttStopId ) restored the lookup. Post-fix verification against production data: 18,002 substitutions applied across 2,199 trips . Timeline 2026-10-05 UAT Pass 2 audit reports 2b-ii "verified and active" based on 73 mature cells in segments.json . No functional test performed. 2026-10-06 ~11:10 UAT Pass 3 finds 2b-ii inert. Defect D1: fetchTimingCells() stored the segments.json document envelope ( {schema, built_at, cells, segments} ); applyEmpiricalBaseline() expected the flat cell map. The hasCells gate could never pass. 2026-10-06 ~11:10 Same pass finds D2: 0 of 154 cells match schedule-adjacent stop pairs — all span multiple stops. 2026-10-06 ~11:20 D1 fixed (unwrap d.segments ). D2 addressed client-side with a covering-span lookup and schedule-proportioned apportioning. Deployed as stamp v20261006-1115 and reported as "2b-ii actually engaging." 2026-10-06 ~11:31 Independent accuracy review reports a stop-ID space mismatch between the detector reference and the timetable (cell 60|741|764 vs timetable stop 741 on route 68) and prescribes a pipeline rebuild. 2026-10-06 ~11:35 Direct GTFS verification ( stop_times.txt , feed S1000182): GTFS stops 741 and 764 are both served by route 60. The cell was correctly keyed. The review compared timetable page indices to GTFS stop IDs as one space — the same category error as the D2 analysis. 2026-10-06 ~11:40 Root cause identified in build-timetable.py : timetable stops arrays store page indices ( stop_to_idx ), not GTFS IDs. Timetable page 741 = GTFS stop 846 (Freud & St Jean, route 68). Client lookups used page indices against GTFS-keyed cells. 2026-10-06 ~11:45 Fix deployed: ttStopId() translates page index → GTFS stop_id via the loaded stopData array, applied to exact and spanning-span lookups. Stamp v20261006-1145 . Served bytes verified. 2026-10-06 ~11:50 Node verification on production data (real timetable, real stopData , real cells, wkd_pm bucket): 18,002 substitutions, 2,199 trips with baselines. Root cause Two distinct numeric ID spaces overlap in range but identify different stops: GTFS stop_id (e.g. "741" = Evergreen & 10 Mile): used by the telemetry detector, reference/route-stops.json , and timing-cell keys ( route|from|to|bucket ). Page index (e.g. 741 = position 741 in the ddot-routes-3d.json stops array = GTFS "846" , Freud & St Jean): used by ddot-timetable-S1000182.json trip stop lists. applyEmpiricalBaseline() concatenated timetable page indices directly into cell keys. Every lookup missed. The failure was silent: the hasCells gate (fixed by D1) passed, the spanning-span scan (added by D2) ran, but stopPos was keyed by page index while cell keys carried GTFS IDs, so no span ever matched either. Why it took three passes Pass 2 inferred "active" from cell count , never executing the lookup path. Count of data is not evidence of function. D1 was a real bug (envelope unwrap) but fixing it only moved the failure one layer down — lookups then ran and still missed. D2 and the accuracy review both assumed the numeric IDs were one space. The D2 fix (spanning-span apportioning) was correct logic applied to wrong keys; the review's "pipeline rebuild" prescription would not have fixed anything, since the pipeline was correct. Resolution came from reading build-timetable.py ( stop_to_idx ) and cross-checking one cell against GTFS stop_times.txt — from the data, not from re-reading the client code. Resolution live-transit.js : ttStopId(pageIdx) → String(stopData[pageIdx].id) , applied in applyEmpiricalBaseline() exact and span lookups. empiricalSpeed() required no change (client map-matched segments already carry GTFS IDs). raptor.js required no change (already consumed depL2 / arrL2 and marked provenance: 'empirical' ). scripts/build_timing.py (transit-data repo): ghost-route traversals no longer emitted as segment.traversed — a latent contamination vector from the accuracy review. Existing cells verified clean (145/145). No reference rebuild was required. The detector reference and pipeline were correct throughout. Verification node --check clean on both changed files. Unit: apportioning logic produced [0, 150, 390, 615] on a synthetic 4-stop trip (exact cell + spanning cell). Production data: 18,002 substitutions / 2,199 trips (40 patterns, wkd_pm). Pair-delta distribution: p50 0.0s, p90 2.0s, p99 157.3s. Largest delta (1647.9s, route 12 pair 5664→5321, scheduled 24s) traced to cell 12|5664|5321|wkd_pm , n=3, mean 1671.9s / p50 1723.3s / p90 1798.4s — three concordant observations of a ~28-minute dwell. The substitution is honest; the schedule was the fiction. Served bytes verified: HTML references live-transit.js?v=20261006-1145 ; JS contains the ttStopId translation. Lessons A count of data is not evidence of function. Pass 2's "73 mature cells, therefore active" was the original error. Functional verification — execute the lookup, count substitutions — is the bar. Overlapping numeric ranges are not one ID space. Page indices and GTFS IDs are both small integers; nothing in the client code marked which was which. The ttStopId comment now records the distinction at the use site. Two independent wrong diagnoses can agree. The D2 analysis and the review's defect-2 analysis made the same category error from different directions. Agreement between analyses is not validation; the GTFS cross-check was. Fix the layer that's actually broken. The pipeline-rebuild prescription was a large, disruptive change to a correct system. Reading the builder showed the translation belonged in the client. Silent fallbacks need tripwires. 2b-ii failed safe (scheduled times) for its entire life, which is why the inertness went unnoticed. A substitution counter existed but was never surfaced. Logging substitution counts where they can be observed is the follow-up. ← Live Transit Detroit series index

pages.title: Belle Isle, Rendered — True-Form Island Geometry for Live Transit — Live Transit Detroit
pages.description: DDOT route 12 serves Belle Isle, but the Live Transit map rendered no island. Build notes on sourcing the true OSM outline, verifying it against GTFS stops, and shipping it as an optional static layer.
pages.text: Belle Isle, Rendered — True-Form Island Geometry for Live Transit — Live Transit Detroit · Detroit Automation Academy Live Transit Detroit · Installment 03 · October 2026 Belle Isle, Rendered Published October 7, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith DDOT route 12 (Conant) serves Belle Isle. The GTFS data carries 24 stops in the island's bounding box, and 20 of the route's 79 path points sit on the island itself — including the Inselruhe interior stops. But the Live Transit map rendered no island at all: the ground is a single dark plane, the Detroit River is not drawn as water, and Belle Isle was not drawn as land. Route 12's ribbon drove across undifferentiated ground — service to a place that did not exist on the map. The gap, precisely The map's geography layers were: a uniform ground plane ( 0x0d1319 ), tiered OSM street geometry, route ribbons, stops, and landmark massing. Water was never rendered, so the island had no visual context — and no island polygon existed in any data file. The route and stop data were correct; the landmass was absent. This is the honest-render rule working as intended: the data said service exists, the map did not show the place, so the map was wrong. What shipped Change What it does Island outline True-form OSM boundary (Nominatim leisure=nature_reserve ), 488 points, pre-projected to the page's coordinate system in assets/belle-isle.json . Verification Polygon triangulates to 486 faces; area ~3.66 km². Both island-interior GTFS stops ("Inselruhe & Loiter Way", "Inselruhe & Riverbank") fall inside; all mainland Jefferson stops fall outside. 20 of 79 route-12 path points land on the island. Rendering Filled landmass at y=3 — above the ground plane, below the street tiers — in dark park-green, with a shoreline stroke and a floating "Belle Isle" place label on a tether, the same label treatment as the People Mover layer. Optional layer Fetched independently of the route data. If the file is absent, the map renders without the island. No failure path, no blocking. Verification Served bytes confirmed before this article published: the page references JS stamp v20261007-0715 , the served JS contains the island builder, and assets/belle-isle.json serves 200 with 489 polygon points. A full two-level UAT round (smoke + interactive: island shape, label, route-12 ribbon, follow-camera behavior) ran against the production build. Shipped with The Belle Isle layer rode the v20261007-0715 promotion with three follow-camera fixes from the same morning's reports: cursor-anchored zoom now disables while tracking (it was re-anchoring the orbit target off the bus), the selected bus no longer shows a redundant route badge, and the Follow OFF toggle survives re-tapping the same bus. Open items The Detroit River itself is still not rendered as water — the island currently sits on the dark ground plane. A river polygon is the natural next geography layer. Mobile verification of the follow-camera fixes has no automated path; on-device testing is the only coverage. SMART live feed remains blocked on the Swiftly API key. ← Live Transit Detroit series index

headings: What this means for the map
pages.text: Beyond 8 Mile — Live Transit Detroit Live Transit Detroit · Installment 05 · October 2026 Beyond 8 Mile Published October 11, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith Eight Mile Road is Detroit's most loaded boundary — the line between the city and the suburbs, and until tonight, the edge of the Live Transit map. Beyond it: nothing. Five changes shipped to production tonight, and the first is that the street mosaic now covers the full SMART service area instead of stopping at the city line. Every SMART visual renders in one red. The SMART filter ships off by default, labeled beta, with its limits stated on the panel. And route ribbons are smoothed at every zoom. Each change was verified against served bytes and live renders before shipping; the verification is documented below. What shipped Change What it does Street mosaic expansion The street layer was regenerated from TIGER/Line 2025 for a wider box — west to lon -83.385, south to lat 42.178 — reaching the western suburbs and Downriver, covering all 270 SMART stops with margin. 38,342 segments (up from ~32,618); the file shrank from 1.25 MB to 1.2 MB through tighter encoding. Full three-tier coverage (freeway, arterial, local) across the entire area. Fade transition Detroit streets stay always-on. The suburban layer fades in over 900 ms when the SMART group toggles on and fades out when it toggles off — mid-fade re-toggles reverse from the current opacity, so the layer never pops. The dashed amber coverage border expands with it, and "routes near you" now works in the suburbs while SMART is on. All-SMART red Every SMART visual — route lines, bus markers, stop pylons, map labels, filter chips — now renders in SMART's brand red #c30915 . Routes 261 and 125 previously rendered in purple ( #A855F7 ) and teal ( #14B8A6 ); those assignments are retired. Implemented as a single color override where the SMART data merges in, so no downstream consumer can keep an old color. SMART (beta), off by default The 45-route SMART group ships toggled off on first load, labeled "SMART (beta)", with the disclaimer: "Beta: 2 of 45 routes have map lines so far. Vehicle positions via the Transit API." The toggle choice persists between visits. When off, zero Transit-derived artifacts render — no lines, no markers, no badge. Verified: 25 buses with SMART off, 89 with it on, back to exactly 25 when toggled off again, no leftovers. Ribbon smoothing Route ribbons were built as straight segments between sparse shape points — 90.6% of joints turned more than 5°, 42% more than 30° — producing a blocky plank-joint look at intermediate zoom. Two iterations of Chaikin subdivision (4× point density) plus true angle-bisector miter joins now render every curve as a smooth continuous ribbon with constant width through bends. Colors, widths, glow, and lighting are unchanged. SMART enabled on the production build: route content renders in SMART red. Render captured during verification. Verification Served bytes confirmed on production: live-transit.js stamp v20261010-2345 containing the Chaikin/miter functions, the SMART_BOUNDS street partition and fade controller, the SMART-red override, and the beta filter persistence; assets/detroit-streets.json serving 1,198,675 bytes with the expanded bounding box and 38,342 segments. Live renders confirmed: the fade in/out with mid-fade reversal, all 45 SMART filter chips rendering #c30915 , smooth ribbons at intermediate zoom, and the off-toggle leaving zero SMART artifacts. Syntax-checked before push; no remaining references to the old purple/teal route colors. What this means for the map The map no longer ends at the city line. SMART's 270 suburban stops — previously floating over unmapped dark, west and south of any road — now sit on a street grid that arrives and departs with the SMART toggle. The honest framing stays: 43 of 45 SMART routes still await line geometry, and the beta label states that on the filter panel. Route-line geometry for the remaining routes is the next backfill. ← Live Transit Detroit series index

pages.title: The People Mover Is Under Construction — Live Transit Detroit
pages.description: The Live Transit map rebuilt its People Mover layer as what the system actually is: an elevated, automated, single-track loop. Build notes on the rework, plus the real system's published downtime and the DTC expansion study.
headings: The People Mover Is Under Construction
What this means for the map
pages.text: The People Mover Is Under Construction — Live Transit Detroit · Detroit Automation Academy Live Transit Detroit · Installment 04 · October 2026 The People Mover Is Under Construction Published October 9, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith The Live Transit map rendered the Detroit People Mover as a 40-meter-wide concrete deck with a solid skirt wall hanging below it — a ground-level corridor drawn through downtown. The real system is none of those things. In the Detroit Transportation Corporation's own words, from its December 2025 system plan: "The DPM is an elevated rail system serving 13 stations in Downtown Detroit. As an automated people mover (APM), the system's driverless two-car trains rely on an automated train control system to complete its 2.9-mile one-way loop." The render was lying about the infrastructure. This build corrects it, and the layer now ships off by default — which is also the honest state of the real system, documented below. Cadillac Center station, elevated, with a two-car train departing. Photo: 42-BRT, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. What shipped Change What it does Off by default The loop no longer renders on load. The filter panel's People Mover toggle enables it. Rationale: the layer is static geometry with no live feed, and the real system has spent much of the last two years closed. 14 m single-track guideway Deck narrowed from 40 m to 14 m — a single automated guideway, not a bus corridor. Narrow enough that street-level stops, buses, and buildings stay visible beneath it. Skirt removed The continuous dark wall below the deck is gone. It was the element obscuring ground objects; open air now sits under the elevated line, as it does in reality. Pillars at stations only Support columns render exclusively at station locations — the known points. No invented infill between them. Station tap priority People Mover station taps are now evaluated before the DDOT stop fallbacks. Downtown DDOT stops were stealing taps aimed at the elevated pins, which read as "stations not selectable." The real guideway: a narrow elevated concrete deck on pillars, open air beneath. Photo: Kyah117, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Verification Served bytes confirmed: the page references JS stamp v20261009-0910 , the served JS contains the narrowed guideway and the off-by-default flag, and the station-picking order change is present in the click handler. Syntax-checked before push; no remaining references to the old 40 m deck width. The real system's published downtime The render change is downstream of a physical fact: the People Mover has been under construction, repeatedly, in public view. DTC's study puts the scale in context: "In both fiscal year (FY) 2024 and 2025, over one million riders used the system to get to their destinations or to explore Downtown Detroit." September 3 – November 22, 2024: an 11-week closure for track replacement — 7,000 feet of rail across nine curves, the worst wear at the Renaissance Center and Greektown curves. Only the third rail replacement in the system's 37-year history (prior: 2008, 2016). Cost near $5 million, funded by state and federal grants; the new rail is expected to last 15–30 years. Source: WDIV; DTC's own project page records it as the "Track Improvement Project and closure from September 3—November 22, 2024." March 13 – May 6, 2026: a seven-week closure after high winds drove sheet metal into the guideway, tearing track cable and damaging switch mechanisms. The system reopened May 6 after 16 days of test runs. DTC CEO and General Manager Melia Howard: "Rider safety is always at the heart of what we do, and it is our responsibility as a public transit provider." Source: Detroit Free Press. The proposed expansion The Detroit Transportation Corporation released its People Mover system plan and downtown mobility study in August 2026 (an $800,000 MDOT grant, roughly eighteen months of work). The study's baseline framing: "Completing a full circuit takes about 15 minutes. The DPM currently runs in a counterclockwise loop but can be operated in either direction." It names three candidate corridors: west to Corktown and Michigan Central, north past the stadiums into Eastern Market, and along the west riverfront to Ralph C. Wilson Jr. Centennial Park. None has funding or a schedule; MDOT is funding the alternatives analysis that would select a route, stations, vehicle type, and payment mechanism. An earlier proposal — doubling the route up Woodward to New Center at $150–200 million — was superseded by the QLine streetcar, which opened in 2017. Separately, DTC plans to replace the 12 original 1986 Mark I cars with 12 refurbished cars of the same model from Toronto's decommissioned Scarborough RT. Sources: DTC system plan (Dec 2025); rawdetroit.org; Wikipedia. What this means for the map The People Mover layer is now drawn the way the system exists: elevated, narrow, automated, one direction — and switched off until the viewer asks for it. If the expansion corridors advance past study into funded construction, the layer will grow with them. Until then, the map declines to present a static loop as a live one. Simulation: real-time information, including construction The layer system that made this rework possible is also the platform's simulation surface. Because the People Mover is static geometry with no live feed, it is the cleanest demonstration of the principle: service states — closures, detours, construction zones, the 2024 track replacement, the 2026 wind-damage shutdown — can be modeled as layer states against the same geometry, with the same provenance labeling the map already carries. The trip planner's scheduled-vs-typical modes are the first consumer of that idea. The next step is construction-aware routing: when a guideway closes for eleven weeks, the map should show the closure, not just the absence. Sources Detroit Transportation Corporation: "Detroit People Mover — System Plan and Downtown Mobility Study, Existing Conditions Assessment" (final, Dec 2025; PDF author: DTC) — system characterization, ridership, loop operation quotes DTC: 2024 Track Improvement Project page — "Track Improvement Project and closure from September 3—November 22, 2024" — thepeoplemover.com WDIV: "People Mover closed for track replacement project in Downtown Detroit" (Sept 3, 2024) — gmg-wdiv-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com Detroit Free Press: "Detroit People Mover reopens seven weeks after wind damage" (May 6, 2026; quotes DTC CEO Melia Howard) — freep.com rawdetroit.org: "People Mover Expansion: Final Plan Maps Routes to Corktown, Eastern Market and the Riverfront" (Oct 2026) — rawdetroit.org Wikipedia: "Detroit People Mover" (expansion proposals; rolling stock) — en.wikipedia.org ← Live Transit Detroit series index

pages.title: QLINE Streetcars Now Live on Live Transit Detroit
pages.description: Press release, October 14, 2026: The QLINE streetcar is live on Live Transit Detroit, on its real GTFS track alignments, with all 12 stations — and the map's stop registry is complete at 10,583 stops across DDOT, SMART, and the QLINE.
headings: QLINE Streetcars Now Live on Live Transit Detroit's 3D Map — on Their Real Track Alignments
pages.text: QLINE Streetcars Now Live on Live Transit Detroit — Detroit Automation Academy Live Transit Detroit · Press release · October 2026 QLINE Streetcars Now Live on Live Transit Detroit's 3D Map — on Their Real Track Alignments Press release · Published October 14, 2026 · Detroit Automation Academy Detroit, MI — October 14, 2026 — Detroit Automation Academy announced that the QLINE streetcar is live on Live Transit Detroit, the academy's real-time 3D transit map, with live streetcar positions running alongside DDOT and SMART buses at detroitautomationacademy.com/live-transit.html . The QLINE is a streetcar line on Woodward Avenue, running 3.3 miles each way between Congress Street downtown and Grand Boulevard in New Center, with 12 stations (sources: Railway Gazette International; M-1 Rail via MapQuest). It opened to the public on May 12, 2017 and is operated by the nonprofit M-1 Rail. The streetcar's place on the map is built from the QLINE's own published GTFS data. All 12 stations — 22 station stops, counting each direction — appear at their platform locations along the QLINE's actual track alignments, including the Grand Boulevard terminus and the downtown terminal loop. Every station stop on the map sits within 4 meters of the track alignment in the QLINE's own data. Live streetcar positions come from the QLINE's public GTFS real-time feed, which publishes vehicle locations with no API key required. The streetcar appears as its own transit mode, distinct from bus markers. It also completes the map's stop registry: as of October 14, Live Transit Detroit carries 10,583 stops across the three agencies — DDOT (5,124), SMART (5,437), and the QLINE (22) — with each stop's routes drawn from the agencies' published GTFS, from downtown Detroit to the end of SMART's suburban network. One part of this work deserves a plain statement: SMART's side of it was made excruciatingly difficult by the agency's refusal to answer. DDOT and the QLINE publish their real-time data openly. SMART's does not reach this map directly, because the durable route — a GTFS real-time API key through Swiftly, the platform that hosts SMART's real-time feed — requires SMART's approval, and no approval or answer has come. The academy's first inquiry, submitted October 2, drew an automated acknowledgment from Swiftly's marketing system — "A member of our team will reach out shortly to schedule a meeting" — and that is the only message Swiftly has ever sent the academy; twelve days later, no human reply has arrived. A formal key request followed on October 13 through Swiftly's API access process, which states that Swiftly will confer with SMART before any key is issued; as of today, no key has been issued. Until SMART answers, its live bus positions reach the map only through a third-party fallback whose coverage resets and rebuilds by design — which is why SMART remains the one agency whose live positions the map cannot yet serve at full reliability. The schedules are not the obstacle: all 45 SMART routes and all 5,437 SMART stops are on the map. It is the live feed that waits on SMART. The map labels routes by name over number — for example, "Fast Michigan - 261" — and sorts route lists alphabetically by name. The QLINE has no route number; it is identified by name only, so it appears on the map simply as "QLINE," labeled as a streetcar. Live Transit Detroit is built and maintained by Detroit Automation Academy, the youth robotics and automation program founded by Justin Spencer Smith. The map tracks every DDOT bus in service and all 45 SMART routes. The academy's thanks to the AI fleet whose testing and debugging carried this launch — the sign error, the street centerline standing in for a track, and the marker capacity cap were each found and fixed along the way. ### Detroit Automation Academy is a Detroit-based youth STEM program teaching robotics, automation, and applied technology. Live Transit Detroit is its public real-time transit visualization project. Media contact: dbkr@umich.edu. ← Live Transit Detroit series index

pages.title: The QLINE Sign Error — Live Transit Detroit
pages.description: The QLINE track rendered as a floating diagonal bar, mirrored kilometres north of Woodward Avenue. Cause: a sign error in one coordinate of qline-3d.json. Resolution: a 64-character data fix, verified numerically and on device.
headings: Why the earlier fix did not fix it
pages.text: The QLINE Sign Error — Live Transit Detroit Live Transit Detroit · Installment 06 · October 2026 The QLINE Sign Error Published October 13, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith On October 12, the QLINE track on the Live Transit map was redrawn from the TIGER/Line 2025 Woodward Avenue centerline, replacing hand-drawn geometry that sat off the road. On October 13, a screenshot from the production page showed the replacement was also wrong: with QLINE enabled, the track rendered as a thick teal bar floating diagonally across the street grid, while the three QLINE vehicle markers sat in their correct positions near Woodward Avenue, south of the bar. This document records the cause of the error, the evidence that isolated it, and the resolution. The fault was one missing minus sign, applied 64 times. Before: the QLINE line rendered as a diagonal bar offset from the street grid. The vehicle markers below it are in their correct positions. Production screenshot, October 13, 2026. The format convention Route geometry for the map is stored in per-agency data files ( ddot-routes-3d.json , smart-routes-3d.json , qline-3d.json ) that share one shape: a projection block, route groups, and routes whose paths are lists of coordinate pairs. The pairs are not latitude and longitude. They are scene coordinates produced by the renderer's projection, project(lat, lon) = [(lon − lon0) · mLon, −(lat − lat0) · mLat] , with mLat = 111320 and the origin at lat0 = 42.381161 . The renderer consumes the pairs verbatim as scene (x, z). The operative consequence is the second coordinate: z = −(lat − lat0) · 111320 . Every point in Detroit is south of the origin parallel, so every valid z in these files is positive — downtown points in the DDOT and SMART files carry z of roughly +5,400 to +5,700. A file that stores z without the negation does not store an approximation of the track. It stores the track's mirror image. Cause of error The October 12 extraction converted the TIGER/Line centerline into the file format and wrote the second coordinate as z = (lat − lat0) · 111320 — projected Y, positive northward — without negating it into scene Z. All 64 points in qline-3d.json (two paths of 32 points; the second path is the first in reverse) therefore carried negative z. The renderer, applying the pairs verbatim, drew the track mirrored across the parallel through the origin: up to approximately 11.5 km too far north, with its north–south slope inverted, which is what produced a diagonal bar crossing the grid instead of a line following the avenue. The x coordinates (longitude) were correct throughout, which is why the bar still crossed Woodward Avenue's longitude band and passed near the corridor at one end. The TIGER/Line centerline geometry itself was sound. Only the conversion into the file format was wrong. Why the earlier fix did not fix it The October 12 change replaced the geometry and reused the same conversion that had produced the hand-drawn file's coordinates. Replacing the input data cannot correct an error in the transformation applied to it. The change was also never verified in a browser on the production page; served-byte checks confirmed that the new file was live, and the file was live — it was the content that was wrong. Both failure modes are recorded in the production rules below. Evidence The diagnosis was reproduced numerically before any change was made, using the renderer's own projection math against the file actually served from production. Unprojecting the served path returned latitudes 42.393–42.433 — north of Grand Boulevard, where Woodward Avenue does not run. Three alternative explanations were tested and eliminated: the served file was byte-identical to the repository file, so the defect was not staleness or caching; the deploy workflow copies root *.json , so the file was being served; and QLINE merges into the same data structure and the same ribbon builder as DDOT and SMART, so the renderer was not treating it differently — the two sibling files render correctly on the same code path. Check As served After the fix Campus Martius to path 7,183 m 37.2 m Grand Circus Park to path 6,587 m 12.3 m Fox Theatre to path 6,297 m 4.3 m Grand Blvd & Woodward to path 2,761 m 7.8 m Live vehicle 287 to path 4,780 m 10.0 m Live vehicle 292 to path 4,592 m 6.5 m Path vs. DDOT route 4 (Woodward, GTFS-derived) mean 3,339 m mean 7.1 m, max 62.2 m Distances are point-to-segment, measured in Node with the production projection. The Congress Street reference measures 141.5 m after the fix; that reference is the centre of the Congress/Woodward intersection, and the track's southern terminus sits on Woodward between Congress and Larned, so a residual offset at that one reference is expected rather than anomalous. Resolution The fix was applied at the data layer only: the second coordinate of all 64 points in qline-3d.json was negated. The renderer was not changed — it and both sibling files agree on the convention, and changing the renderer to match one incorrect file would have broken every correct one. No geometry was rebuilt; the TIGER/Line points were already correct once the sign convention was honoured. The byte-level diff against the previous file is exactly the 64 removed minus signs (1,637 → 1,573 bytes); the projection block, groups, stops, and metadata are untouched, and no JavaScript changed, so no cache stamp moved. The change shipped as commit 59c99261cb to the production repository on GitHub Pages; the deployment for that commit reported success, and the file served at the production URL is byte-identical to the fixed file. After: the QLINE line lies on the Woodward corridor, the label anchors over midtown, and the vehicle markers sit on the line. Production screenshot, October 13, 2026. Verification After the fix, the path unprojects to latitudes 42.329–42.369, monotonic from the Congress Street end to Grand Boulevard, with endpoints at (42.32937, −83.04530) and (42.36912, −83.07257) — Woodward Avenue at both termini. Two of the three live QLINE vehicles measured 10.0 m and 6.5 m from the corrected path. The third sat approximately 330 m beyond the northern endpoint, consistent with terminus turnback and layover trackage at Grand Boulevard, which the extracted revenue alignment does not include; it does not affect the drawn route. Visual confirmation was completed on device against the production page: the line lies on Woodward Avenue for its full length, the QLINE label anchors over the corridor, and the DDOT and SMART lines are unchanged. Rules recorded Two standing rules come out of this defect. First, before replacing any data file, read the existing file's byte structure and the consumer's parsing code — and where sibling files follow a convention, verify the new file against a sibling that renders correctly; a sign convention is exactly the class of detail that "same JSON shape" does not capture. Second, a geometry change is not done when it is pushed or when the served bytes match. It is done when the rendered result has been seen on the production page. The October 12 change satisfied the first two checks and was still wrong in the only way that mattered. ← Live Transit Detroit series index

pages.title: Build Notes: October 6 Promotion — Nine Changes to Production — Live Transit Detroit
pages.description: Build notes for the October 6, 2026 Live Transit promotion: transition engine, Kalman-filtered bus motion, landmark massing, and depth-ordered tap picking — verified through two UAT levels before reaching production.
pages.text: Build Notes: October 6 Promotion — Nine Changes to Production — Live Transit Detroit · Detroit Automation Academy Live Transit Detroit · Installment 02 · October 2026 Build Notes: October 6 Promotion Published October 6, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith Nine changes moved from staging to the production Live Transit page today, in two promotions ( v20261006-1815 and v20261006-2120 ). Every change passed a 16-check staging UAT and a two-level production UAT before serving. Two defects found during UAT were fixed before promotion. This is the record. What shipped Change What it does Marker redesign Bus pillars 620m → 220m; glow, core, beacon, and ground ring rescaled to match. Pillars no longer tower over the downtown buildings they stand beside. DisplayBounds Measures viewport, device class, edge insets, and on-screen chrome per frame; exposes the safe frame every camera move must respect. Debug readout at ?dbdebug=1 , hostname-gated to staging. TransitionEngine Central camera-transition controller. Bus selection glides to a 32° vantage at the safe-frame center; pointer input cancels immediately; cancelled transitions never engage follow. Mobile gets a compact bus bar, frame-and-hold, and an explicit Follow toggle; desktop auto-follows on natural completion. Minimum-jerk easing Camera tweens now use the quintic t³(6t²−15t+10) profile — zero velocity and acceleration at both endpoints — replacing ease-in-out cubic. Badge decluttering Greedy screen-space placement for route badges; selected bus prioritized, stable slot order, spiral candidate search. Clustered badges stay individually legible. Kalman motion + halos Per-bus Kalman filter (arc position, velocity, covariance; 15m GPS sigma) replaces raw dead reckoning. Uncertainty renders as a soft disc of radius 3σ, clamped 15–150m, opacity 0.16. Stop camera intent Selecting a stop glides the camera to a 700m, 32° stop vantage with no follow. Previously the card opened and the camera stayed put. Depth-ordered tap picking One raycast across bus and stop meshes; the frontmost marker wins. Previously buses were tested first and always won, so a stop standing in front of a bus pillar could not be selected. Found from an on-device report, fixed same day. Landmark massing (Phase A) True-form OSM building massing for downtown Detroit — 6,981 vertices, 6,753 triangles, one merged draw call, 272KB. High fidelity reserved for close zoom; progressive detail is Phase B. Verification Staging UAT (16 checks, automated browser, read-only): 14 passed. One failure — stop selection never moved the camera — root-caused to an unmigrated Phase 2 intent and fixed before promotion. Mobile checks could not run (no viewport emulation in the test harness). Production UAT, Level 1 (smoke): 6/6 passed — clean load, correct stamp, 72 live buses, landmarks serving, no errors, feed live. It also caught a stale hardcoded build string in the help footer, fixed in a follow-up commit. Production UAT, Level 2 (interactive): bus selection, glide, follow, card close, badge legibility, and stop glide all passed. Depth-ordered picking and the trip planner received partial verification; mobile remains untested in automation. Every deploy was verified by served bytes, not by workflow success: the HTML stamp, the JS feature markers, and the landmarks payload were each fetched from the live URL and confirmed. Also fixed today Telemetry pipeline race. The 5-minute logger and the timing-model builder both write data/timing/segments.json ; a logger commit landing mid-build broke the builder's rebase. The commit step is now conflict-proof: on rebase conflict it aborts, rebuilds on the new tip (watermark-idempotent), and retries the push. Stop label stacking. Production screenshots showed stop name labels piling into unreadable stacks at street zoom. The greedy screen-space collision used for street labels now applies to stop labels. Build string drift. The help footer carried a hardcoded build number that went stale for days. It now derives from the cache stamp at load. Open items Mobile verification (compact bar, frame-and-hold, Follow toggle) has no automated path; on-device testing is the only coverage. Landmark Phase B (progressive LOD) is designed, not implemented. SMART live feed remains blocked on the Swiftly API key. ← Live Transit Detroit series index

pages.title: The Invisible Middle Leg — Live Transit Detroit
pages.description: A completed case study of two-transfer invisibility in Detroit transit routing: across a 630-instance census and a predeclared measurement, two-transfer optima are invisible to Google at a frame-weighted rate of 0.89 (descriptive range 0.56–0.97) and to Moovit at 0.78 (0.44–0.94), while one-transfer controls are surfaced 7 times in 8.
headings: 2. The census: how much of the network rides on journeys like this
3. The rate phase, designed before it was run
7. The rule the study runs under
pages.text: The Invisible Middle Leg — Live Transit Detroit Live Transit Detroit · Installment 07 · October 2026 The Invisible Middle Leg October 16, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith On the scheduled timetable, the fastest way from the Providence hospital campus at Greenfield & 9 Mile to Woodward & Warren leaves at 12:45 PM and arrives at 1:42 PM: three buses, two transfers, 57 minutes. No external routing engine offered that journey. Google's best arrival for the trip was 1:55 PM, the DDOT journey planner's 1:59 PM, Moovit's 2:01 PM — and DDOT route 3, the middle leg that makes the fast journey work, appeared in none of the 25 itineraries the three engines returned between them. This installment is the completed case study that began with that trip. It asks whether the Providence result was an accident of one origin–destination pair, and it answers the question in three stages: a census of the whole network's optimal journeys, computed from the timetable alone; a demonstration stage that measured what engines show for the census's largest-margin journeys; and a rate phase, designed and fixed in writing before any of its captures ran, that measured how often the two-transfer class of journeys is invisible. The finding is specific. Direct and one-transfer optima are surfaced by both independent engines essentially every time they were measured — in the demonstration stage, at rank 1 in all 14 surfacings. Two-transfer optima are invisible at frame-weighted rates of 0.89 (Google; descriptive range 0.56–0.97) and 0.78 (Moovit; 0.44–0.94) — and every one of the 24 two-transfer optima in the measured sample was invisible to at least one of the two engines (24 of 24 in this sample; that disjointness is a property of the sample, not a frame rate). Defined terms The terms below are used in this installment only in these senses. Each definition is the study record's own (phase-rate.md §§1–5 and its addendum; rate-phase-analysis.md as corrected; phase-generalization.md for the census terms). Native planner The Live Transit app's own planner engine, computing journeys from the DDOT GTFS timetable (feed S1000182, scheduled times) alone. Every "native" figure in this study is its output; no external engine's output enters it (§7). Native journey; optimum The journey the native planner returns for an instance: the earliest-arriving journey under the planner's own rules — at most 2 transfers, at most 30 minutes of cumulative walking, walk transfers within the feed's 400 m graph. "Optimal" throughout means planner-optimal in this sense. Instance One measurement unit of the census: a (departure slot, origin node, destination node) triple. The census holds 630 instances; the rate phase's frame, sample, and controls are all instances. Leg One route's ride within a journey, from boarding to alighting. A journey of one leg is direct; two legs make one transfer; three legs make two transfers. Middle leg In a three-leg journey, the second leg — the one between the two transfers. Route sequence A journey written as its ordered routes: 10-3-8 is route 10, then route 3, then route 8. Sequence matching ignores walk legs and presentation; an itinerary containing SMART routes is a different sequence — recorded as offered in its own right, never as a match. Sequence invisibility; offered / not offered The study's primary outcome, per instance and engine. An engine is scored offered when the native route sequence appears among its itineraries at the instance's matched departure, at any rank (for Moovit, at any display position across its sections); otherwise the native journey is invisible to that engine for that instance — recorded as not offered . Leg margin For a leg of the optimal journey: the best arrival with that leg's route removed from the timetable and the journey fully re-optimized, minus the optimal arrival. A margin of null — no journey exists without the route — is unbounded. Load-bearing leg A leg with a margin of 5 minutes or more, or with no journey existing without it (infeasible). The substitute in the margin test is the best routing the network offers without the leg, not a single named alternative. Journey margin The maximum leg margin over an optimal journey's legs; unbounded if any leg is infeasible. It is the instance-level measure the rate phase stratifies on — a maximum-leg statistic, not a whole-journey margin (§6). Two-transfer optimum An instance whose native journey has exactly two transfers (three legs). The census's 88 two-transfer optima are the class this study measures. Census The generalization phase's computation of the native journey for every instance: 15 significant nodes giving 210 directed pairs, at three departure slots (Thursday 12:45 PM, Thursday 5:15 PM, Saturday 12:45 PM) — 630 instances, computed from the timetable alone. Frame The population the rate phase estimates over: the census's 88 two-transfer optima. Band A stratum of the frame by journey margin: low , under 10 minutes (24 frame instances); median , 10 to under 30 minutes (38); high , 30 minutes or more, or unbounded (26). Sample The 24 two-transfer instances selected for capture: 8 per band, allocated between the load-bearing-middle and non-load-bearing-middle cells in the full frame's proportions for that band (low 3/5, median 5/3, high 6/2), and taken at centered systematic ranks within each cell so the picks span the cell's margin range. The selection is deterministic, with one predeclared adjustment (the Saturday floor, §3) — a stratified selection with known frame weights, not a random draw. Control One of 8 one-transfer optima matched to the two-transfer sample on margin band and departure slot, chosen by closeness of journey margin to the selected two-transfer band medians. The controls are a matched comparison set, not a probability sample of the census's 282 one-transfer optima. Exhibit An instance measured before the rate phase existed, by purposive selection: the Providence study instance and the demonstration instances D1–D8. Exhibits are reported separately, excluded from every pool, and never pooled into any rate. Coverage-explained absence An absence flagged when the engine's best bus arrival is achieved by an itinerary using SMART routes no later than the native arrival; a flag stands when any itinerary achieving that best arrival uses SMART routes. A flagged absence is a coverage case — the engine answered from a different network — not an invisibility case; the primary rate counts it regardless, and the coverage-adjusted rate excludes it. Depart-at The departure specified for an engine query. The protocol sets it to the instance's census departure exactly (Thursday instances at the mapped same-weekday date recorded in §5); when an engine substitutes a different departure, the capture is flagged and not silently scored. Capture One instance measured in one engine under the protocol: origin and destination typed verbatim from the census nodes' specs, depart-at set, and every itinerary the engine offers recorded with its rank, full route sequence, and arrival. The rate phase's workload is 64 captures. Provisional capture A capture flagged in its file as not final because a protocol condition — the departure time or date — was not met as specified. Its verdicts are not scored until a recapture resolves them. Recapture A capture run again under the protocol's exact conditions, replacing a provisional or unreadable original; the protocol allows one recapture per unreadable capture. The two provisional batches were resolved by exact-date recaptures (§5). Superseded The status of a provisional capture once its recapture is final: the provisional file is retained and marked superseded, never edited into agreement, and no superseded verdict feeds any total. Frame-weighted rate (θ) Per engine, θ = Σ (N h / 88) · (x h / n h ) over the three bands, with frame counts N = (24, 38, 26): the bands' invisibility rates combined at the frame's band shares — the estimated proportion of the 88-instance frame that is sequence-invisible to that engine. Descriptive range The range attached to θ wherever it is stated, propagated from the bands' Wilson 95% bounds under the study's design-based framing: 0.56–0.97 for Google, 0.44–0.94 for Moovit. The range is part of the claim — the record supports a rate in that span, not a precise point. 1. The demonstration: Providence → Woodward & Warren The study instance is a stop-to-stop computation on DDOT GTFS feed S1000182, run with the app's own planner engine over the scheduled timetable (Thursday service, ready at the origin stop at 12:45 PM). The origin is the stop "North Park Dr & North Park Pl" on the Providence campus (registry idx 1759); the destination is the timetable-covered stop "Woodward & Warren" (idx 751), which is where the deployed planner resolves the destination. Two routings were compared leg by leg: 10-3-8 — route 10 (Greenfield) → route 3 (Grand River) → route 8 (Warren), two transfers: arrive 1:42 PM, 57 minutes (ride 46 min, wait 8 min, walk 3 min). 10-8 — route 10 → route 8, one transfer: arrive 2:11 PM, 86 minutes (ride 58 min, wait 26 min, walk 2 min). The 29-minute gap is itemized in the record: 18 minutes less waiting, 12 minutes less riding, 1 minute more walking. The wait is the mechanism. The route 10 bus reaches Greenfield & Warren at 1:16 PM and the rider is ready at the route 8 stop at 1:17 PM — two minutes after route 8's 1:15 PM departure. Route 8's departures from Greenfield in the study window are irregular, roughly every 30 minutes, so the one-transfer rider waits 26 minutes for the 1:43 PM bus. The two-transfer rider instead rides route 3 — departing Grand River & Greenfield every 10–12 minutes — and boards that same missed route 8 vehicle further along its run, at Grand River at 1:34 PM, reaching Woodward at 1:41 PM. Across a 13-departure sweep (ready times every 15 minutes from 12:45 PM to 3:45 PM), 10-3-8 never loses to 10-8: it wins three departures (by 29, 26, and 20 minutes) and ties ten. The ties are structural — in those rows both routings board the same route 8 vehicle and arrive together; the wins occur exactly where the Greenfield connection misses a route 8 departure by 2–5 minutes of ready time and the route 3 path recovers it downstream. Against the external engines, at the matched departure: Google's best arrival was 1:55 PM , the DDOT planner's 1:59 PM , and Moovit's 2:01 PM — 13, 17, and 19 minutes after the native best. All three bests are SMART-built itineraries (a coverage difference, recorded as such in the benchmark: the native planner's column is DDOT-only, and a faster SMART answer is a coverage case, not an invisibility case). The DDOT planner is Google-based and is not an independent measurement. What no engine offered, at any rank, was the native sequence: 10-3-8 appears in zero of the 25 itineraries across the three engines, and DDOT route 3 appears in zero of 25 . One precision the generalization phase added, stated here so the demonstration is not over-read: measured against the named alternative 10-8, the stake at this departure is 29 minutes; measured against the best route-3-free re-optimization of the whole network (10-7-4, arriving 1:47 PM), route 3's leg margin at the study instance is 6.8 minutes. Both numbers are correct under their definitions; the study uses the second definition — margin against a fully re-optimized substitute — everywhere after this section. 2. The census: how much of the network rides on journeys like this The generalization phase computed the network's optimal journeys from the timetable alone. Fifteen significant nodes (transit centers, radial corridor anchors, the 8 Mile crosstown line, the study's own geography) give 210 directed pairs; at three departure slots (Thursday 12:45 PM, Thursday 5:15 PM, Saturday 12:45 PM) that is 630 instances , each computed with the app's planner under its own rules (at most 2 transfers, at most 30 minutes of cumulative walking, the feed's 400 m walk-transfer graph, scheduled times). Of the 630 optima, 260 are one bus leg, 282 are two legs, and 88 are three legs — the two-transfer optima that form the class this study is about. For every leg of every optimal journey the planner was re-run with that leg's route removed and the journey fully re-optimized — the re-run that produces each leg's margin and load-bearing status (Defined terms). Across the 630 optima there are 1,083 legs belonging to the optimal journey itself; 752 of the 1,083 (69%) are load-bearing , with a median margin of 10.3 minutes. Most legs in an optimum are not decorative: in this network, the optimal path usually runs on infrastructure with no close substitute. Classified by the journey that carries them, the 752 load-bearing legs divide as: direct journeys 228 (30.3%), one-transfer journeys 335 (44.5%), and two-transfer journeys 189 — 25.1% of all load-bearing legs , carrying 21.1% of the census's finite load-bearing margin. A load-bearing middle leg is the norm in that class, not the exception: 54 of the 88 two-transfer optima (61%) have one, and route 3 alone is a load-bearing middle leg in 18 of the 21 optima where it sits in the middle. The Providence anatomy recurs across the census; it is not a one-corridor accident. The demonstration stage then measured engine behavior on eight instances (D1–D8) selected by native criteria alone — the route in the outright optimum, a large margin, dayparts and corridors spread. The result was exact: the native sequence was surfaced in 7 of 8 instances — 14 of 16 engine-measurements — at rank 1 in both engines every time it was offered , and the tested route appeared somewhere in the set in 16 of 16 measurements. The one miss was total in both engines: D6 (Gratiot & 8 Mile → Woodward & Warren; native 6-31-4), the demonstration pool's only two-transfer instance. Route 6 was present in both engines' sets, paired differently; route 31 appeared in no itinerary from either engine . The failure was a pairing failure — the 6→31 Mack Avenue connection that makes the native optimum is constructed by neither engine. Adding the original study instance — also a two-transfer optimum, also invisible in every engine measured — the whole study's two-transfer demonstration record at that point was 0 sequences surfaced in 5 engine-measurements , against 14 of 14 rank-1 surfacings for the direct and one-transfer classes. The refined claim from that stage, which the rate phase was designed to test, is this: direct and single-transfer load-bearing journeys are universally surfaced — at rank 1 — by every engine measured; the invisible class is the multi-transfer optimum whose connecting middle leg an engine must specifically construct and, in both exhibits on record, does not. What two exhibits could not supply was a rate: the claim rested on 2 instances, and the demonstration pool was the large-margin tail by design, so nothing estimated how engines treat median-margin optima. The rate phase exists to repair exactly those two weaknesses. 3. The rate phase, designed before it was run The rate phase's design — estimands, frame, stratification, measurement protocol, and analysis plan — was written and fixed (phase-rate.md, §§1–9) before any capture for the phase ran. Its machine-readable selection is reproducible from the census alone by a script that reads no engine output. Population and outcome. The frame is the census's 88 two-transfer optima . The primary outcome, per instance and engine, is sequence invisibility : the engine, at the instance's matched departure, does not offer the native route sequence at any rank. Engine visibility is a measured outcome, never an input. Bands. Instances are stratified by journey margin — the maximum leg margin over the optimal journey's legs, unbounded if any leg is infeasible: low, under 10 minutes (24 frame instances); median, 10 to under 30 (38); high, 30 or more or unbounded (26) . Of the 88, 54 have a load-bearing middle leg. Sample. Eight instances per band (24 total), allocated between the load-bearing-middle and non-load-bearing-middle cells in the full frame's proportions for that band (low 3/5, median 5/3, high 6/2 — 14 load-bearing-middle instances in the sample), and taken at centered systematic ranks within each cell so the picks span each cell's margin range rather than repeating the demonstration stage's top-tail draw. One adjustment was declared in the design in advance — a Saturday floor, which replaces a pick when a band's frame holds at least five Saturday instances but its picks hold none; it fired once (R13, median band) and the swap is recorded in that instance's metadata. Controls. Eight one-transfer optima matched to the two-transfer sample on margin band and departure slot, chosen by closeness of journey margin to the selected two-transfer band medians. Seven of the eight match within 6.2 minutes; the eighth (C8, high band, Thursday peak) cannot match closer than 37.86 minutes — no census instance does better — and the distance is printed in the design, not hidden. Exhibits. The Providence study instance and D1–D8 are excluded from every pool. They are reported separately, and are never pooled into any rate. Protocol. Origin and destination typed verbatim from the census nodes' specs; depart-at set to the instance's census departure exactly; every itinerary the engine offers recorded with its rank, full route sequence, and arrival. An absence is flagged coverage-explained when the engine's best bus arrival is achieved by a SMART-route itinerary no later than the native arrival; the primary rate counts sequence absence regardless, and a predeclared sensitivity re-computes the rate excluding coverage-explained absences. An unreadable capture is missing, never scored as absent ; one recapture is allowed. Two further sensitivities were predeclared: missing-data bounds, and an exhibits-included raw count labeled as a description, not an estimate. Primary estimand. Per engine, θ = Σ (N h /88) · (x h /n h ) over the three bands with frame counts N = (24, 38, 26) — the frame-weighted proportion of the 88 two-transfer optima that is sequence-invisible — plus the paired joint rates (invisible to both engines; invisible to at least one), band rates with Wilson 95% intervals, and a cross-tabulation by middle-leg margin and load-bearing-middle status, reported as counts and labeled descriptive. The workload fixed by the design was 32 instances × 2 engines = 64 captures : 48 two-transfer, 16 control. The engines are Google Maps transit directions and Moovit — the two independent engines; the DDOT planner, being Google-based, is not captured as a separate measurement. 4. The rate phase's record includes its own defects, flagged by the capturing operators in the capture files at the time, labeled provisional there, and resolved by exact-date recapture — with the provisional files retained and marked superseded, not edited into agreement. Google batch G2 — wrong clock time. Four Thursday 5:15 PM instances (R10, R11, R14, R16) were captured at 5:00 PM: the depart-at control would not hold 5:15 PM across more than ten attempts. The deviation was flagged in the batch file and all four verdicts marked provisional. Recaptured the same evening at the exact depart-at via the URL epoch parameter, every final page verified on-page. The recapture reversed two verdicts : R14 and R16, recorded as not offered at 5:00 PM, are offered at 5:15 PM at ranks 5 and 6 — both reversals run against the study's hypothesis and in the engines' favor. R10 and R11 were confirmed not offered. Moovit batch M2 — wrong Thursday. Seven Thursday instances were captured on Thursday, October 15 (same weekday, same clock times) instead of the mapped Thursday, October 22, because the operator did not use the URL time-parameter method the other Moovit batches used. All seven verdicts were marked provisional in the file. The exact-date recapture verified "Departure day Thu, Oct 22" and the correct time on every page before recording: all seven outcomes were confirmed (R12 and R15 offered at rank 2; the other five not offered); R15's provisional verdict — offered at rank 2 at 12:45 PM — was confirmed unchanged at the verified exact date. The epoch error. The Moovit recapture task was supplied with epoch values that encode 12:45 and 17:15 UTC; on-page they displayed as 8:45 AM and 1:15 PM EDT — four hours early. The operator caught the discrepancy on the first page, used corrected epochs, and verified the displayed departure on every page. The error and its correction are recorded in the recapture file itself. Final state of the record. 64 of 64 captures final, zero unreadable, zero missing — so the predeclared missing-data bounds collapse to the point estimates (θ G 0.89, θ M 0.78). Depart-at sensitivity is empirical fact within this phase: a departure 15 minutes early hid two sequences that the exact departure shows, and the wrong-Thursday batch's seven verdicts all had to be re-verified at the mapped date before any of them could be scored. That is why the protocol's exactness rules exist, and why provisional captures are never silently scored. Peer review. After the analysis was filed, the rate phase record was reviewed cold by three independent reviewers — statistical methods; measurement and transit-domain validity; reproducibility and record integrity. Every headline number was independently recomputed and found exact; the instance selection was reproduced bit-for-bit from the census by re-running the selection script; no verdict was found mis-scored, and the coverage rule was re-derived in all 41 determinations and found applied as written. The reviews logged 24 defects — all in documentation and claim calibration, none in data. Twenty-two were corrected in the study record: among them, descriptive uncertainty ranges attached to the class rates (§4), the margin-trend statement restated as descriptive with its power caveat (§4), the two recapture files' epoch annotations reconciled (§5), a factual error in the route-3 note's origins corrected (§4), and the R15 supersession narrative corrected to what the provisional file actually recorded (§5). Two were accepted as stated limitations and are recorded in §6. No capture was re-taken and no number moved. The reviews and the defect register are filed with the study record ( peer-review-r1-statistics.md , peer-review-r2-measurement.md , peer-review-r3-reproducibility.md , peer-review-packet.md ). 6. Limitations These are the limits recorded in the design and the analysis, stated without softening. The rates are design-based estimates over this census frame — 15 significant nodes, three departure slots on two days (the peak slot is Thursday-only), scheduled times, the app's planner rules — under the recorded selection rule. They are not sampling-theoretic claims about all possible origin–destination pairs, and sibling-origin instances are correlated (adjacent nodes on the same corridors repeatedly produce identical downstream journeys), so the intervals are descriptive of this frame, not of a trip population. Providence concentration in the high band. 17 of the 26 high-band frame instances touch the Providence node, and 7 of the 24 selected instances do (R14, R16, R20–R24). Providence's only service is route 10, so its journey margins are driven by first- and last-leg access — up to 128.7 minutes, and unbounded on Saturday — not by the middle leg. The band therefore mixes two phenomena, access uniqueness and construction stakes; that is why the mechanism read is the middle-leg cross-tab and not the band. Journey margin is a maximum-leg statistic. It can be set by a leg other than the one whose construction is in question (R21: journey margin 115.0 minutes from its first leg; middle-leg margin 4.2). The design accepts this because it matches the study's earlier instance-margin usage, and compensates with the cross-tab; a future phase could stratify on middle-leg margin directly, at the cost of having no common metric for the one-transfer controls. Two judgment calls in the coverage analysis are recorded, not smoothed over. (1) R19 for Google is flagged coverage-explained under the rule as written, although the same best arrival is co-achieved by a DDOT itinerary (17→30) — the tie is recorded in the analysis. (2) Moovit's R10 is not flagged, because the coverage rule reads the engine's bus itineraries; a Combined-bike itinerary using SMART 561 arrives earlier than the native arrival, and if combined-bike itineraries were counted, R10 would also be coverage-explained and the adjusted Moovit rate would be 0.463 instead of 0.517. Scheduled, not realized. All native figures are timetable figures. The app shifts near-term DDOT times by measured live delay; each engine's schedule vintage and real-time adjustments are unknown throughout this study, as in every stage of it. A margin of an hour survives any plausible adjustment; a margin of five minutes may not. The controls are a matched comparison set , not a probability sample of the census's 282 one-transfer optima; their rate is a benchmark for the contrast, and the high-band control contrast carries C8's recorded 37.86-minute match distance. Result-set exhaustion was not separately demonstrated (accepted limitation, recorded in peer review). The protocol requires result sets to be read in full, but the capture files do not record per-capture itinerary totals or end-of-list confirmations. The absence verdicts rest on the displayed result sets as captured and verified on-page. In two batches the full cross-section display order is recorded (up to 8 entries including bike sections), indicating the lists were read to their ends there, and nothing in any file suggests a truncated read — but the limitation stands, and it is not retro-fixable. Exact re-execution is impossible in principle (accepted limitation, recorded in peer review). No raw engine output was archived — the captures are transcriptions — and both engines are live, non-stationary services whose schedule vintages are unknown. Every quantity the conclusions rest on is filed and recomputes from the record (the peer reviewers did exactly that), but the captures themselves cannot be re-run into the same engine state. "Optimal" means planner-optimal — at most two transfers, at most 30 minutes of cumulative walking, walk transfers within the feed's 400 m graph. A routing outside those rules is outside this census by construction. 7. The rule the study runs under External routing engines' output — Google, Moovit, the DDOT planner, Apple, the Transit app — is for efficiency comparison only. It never becomes an input to the app's native compute engine: no external suggestion, ranking, or routing is ingested, imitated, or used to steer the planner. In this study the rule is operational, not decorative: instance selection and every margin derive solely from the native timetable computation; engine visibility is a measured outcome, never an input; and per the analysis plan's no-feedback clause, nothing in these results alters the selection, the native engine, or any later phase's inputs. Benchmarks measure the difference. They do not close it by contamination. pages.description: Implementing a shared App Group architecture so an iOS app and its Home Screen widget read and write the same SwiftData store — eliminating the empty-widget problem.
headings: Stability through Shared Storage: The App Group Milestone
pages.text: Stability through Shared Storage: The App Group Milestone — Notes · Detroit Automation Academy Notes · iOS · February 2026 Stability through Shared Storage: The App Group Milestone Published February 21, 2026 · Detroit Automation Academy · Historical engineering note — migrated from the retired blog. System stability is non-negotiable. We implemented a shared App Group architecture for the diary app, ensuring seamless data flow between the main application and its Home Screen widget. Shared model container: migrating to a group container identifier eliminated data latency between the app and widget targets. Entitlement alignment: unified the security posture of both the app and the widget to permit real-time read/write access to the core SwiftData store. Reliability: this prevents the "empty widget" syndrome — the widget always reflects the latest data instead of a stale or missing snapshot. This foundational work prepares the app for background-driven features like live location tracking and background photo processing. This is a private project. No App Store release is planned. ← All notes

pages.title: Sprint 2: Building a Privacy-First Diary on Apple Native Frameworks — Notes
pages.description: Why we chose native Apple frameworks over third-party SDKs for a private on-device diary app — MusicKit, EventKit, CoreData with CloudKit, and what privacy-first means in practice.
headings: Sprint 2: Building a Privacy-First Diary on Apple Native Frameworks
pages.text: Sprint 2: Building a Privacy-First Diary on Apple Native Frameworks — Notes · Detroit Automation Academy Notes · iOS · February 2026 Sprint 2: Building a Privacy-First Diary on Apple Native Frameworks Published February 28, 2026 · Detroit Automation Academy · Historical engineering note — migrated from the retired blog. Sprint 2 of the diary app is complete with a successful build. Here's what we shipped and how the architecture decisions are holding up. The core premise Most journaling apps ask you to trust their servers with your most personal data. This one doesn't. Every piece of data it touches — music history, calendar events, location context, photos — is processed on-device and stored with iCloud encryption. Nothing phones home. The framework stack Framework Data domain Privacy approach MusicKit What you're listening to Requests user permission; no data leaves device EventKit Calendar & reminders Read-only access to authorized calendars Contacts Named entities in your day Accessed by identifier only, never bulk imported CoreLocation Where you are Significant location changes only, stored as geohash Photos Visual memory triggers Thumbnails generated locally, originals never read Sprint 2 deliverables MusicKit integration. Authorization flow complete. The app captures the current track at entry creation time. Album artwork is pulled from the MusicKit catalog and displayed as a contextual thumbnail. EventKit read pipeline. Calendar events for the current day are fetched and ranked by duration and proximity to the current time. The top 3 events populate the "Today's Context" section automatically. CoreData + CloudKit persistence. All diary entries are stored in a CoreData stack with CloudKit sync enabled via NSPersistentCloudKitContainer . Entries sync across Apple devices without ever touching a third-party server. Successful build. Clean build against the iOS 18.0 target with zero warnings on all privacy-sensitive framework calls. What's next Entry card design: rich contextual tiles with music, location, and event context Timeline view: chronological scroll with ambient colors derived from album art On-device ML: using CreateML to surface recurring patterns across diary entries This is a private project. No App Store release is planned. ← All notes
