pages.description: Sprint 3: CoreLocation and MapKit integration for spatial context, Photos framework highlights, and on-device narrative generation — without sacrificing the zero-knowledge architecture.
headings: Spatial context: more than just coordinates
pages.text: Sprint 3: Privacy-First Spatial Intelligence — Notes · Detroit Automation Academy Notes · iOS · March 2026 Sprint 3: Privacy-First Spatial Intelligence Published March 3, 2026 · Detroit Automation Academy · Historical engineering note — migrated from the retired blog. A diary isn't just a list of events; it's a narrative of space and time. In Sprint 3, we bridged the gap between raw data and visual storytelling by integrating CoreLocation , MapKit , and the Photos framework . Spatial context: more than just coordinates We implemented a custom location provider that identifies significant locations visited throughout the day. Instead of just logging GPS coordinates, the local processing pipeline turns these into meaningful "Significant Locations" (e.g., "Michigan Central Station" vs. "2001 15th St"). Key achievements in Sprint 3: MapKit integration: the new timeline view features an interactive map showing the day's journey. Privacy-first geofencing: all location processing happens on-device. No location data is sent to external APIs for reverse geocoding; Apple's native frameworks keep the "where" private. Visual context: reliving the moment A photo is worth a thousand words, and in the diary app, it's the anchor of the narrative. We integrated the Photos framework to fetch relevant highlights from the user's library for each diary entry. Dynamic highlights: the diary automatically pairs photos with the locations and events they correspond to. Zero-knowledge photos: we only store local identifiers (PHAsset IDs). The actual image data never leaves the encrypted on-device storage. Narrative generation, on-device The most significant technical leap in this sprint is the upgrade to the summary service. A local model-context server now acts as a compute delegate, generating narratives that weave together: The music you listened to The meetings you attended The places you visited The photos you took The result is a cohesive summary of the day that reads naturally but is entirely automated and private. This is a private project. No App Store release is planned. ← All notes

pages.title: Fixing Our CI/CD Pipeline: Submodules, Empty Commits, and the QA Gate — Notes
pages.description: A post-mortem on recurring deployment failures — Hugo builds that succeeded with missing content, uninitialized theme submodules, and the automated QA gate that caught them.
headings: Fixing Our CI/CD Pipeline: Submodules, Empty Commits, and the QA Gate
pages.text: Fixing Our CI/CD Pipeline: Submodules, Empty Commits, and the QA Gate — Notes · Detroit Automation Academy Notes · DevOps · February 2026 Fixing Our CI/CD Pipeline: Submodules, Empty Commits, and the QA Gate Published February 28, 2026 · Detroit Automation Academy · Historical engineering note — migrated from the retired blog. Our site pipeline had a recurring problem: deployments that worked locally failed silently in GitHub Actions, or succeeded in Actions but produced a broken site. Here's the root cause analysis and what we changed. The three failure modes Build succeeds, site content missing — the output directory was generated but the git commit step failed silently because there was nothing new to commit. The deploy step ran anyway and pushed a stale build. Theme submodule not initialized — the theme is a git submodule. Fresh Actions runners clone the repo but don't automatically initialize submodules. The build proceeded with an empty theme directory, producing an unstyled build that nonetheless exited with code 0. Cache invalidation lag — CDN-cached pages served stale content after a new deployment. Fix 1: Submodule initialization - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: submodules: true # ← this was missing fetch-depth: 0 Without submodules: true , the build finds the theme reference, looks in the theme directory, finds nothing, and falls back to default templates — completely unstyled. Fix 2: The empty commit guard # Before — always commits, fails when nothing changed git add public/ git commit -m "Deploy" git push # After — skips if nothing changed git add public/ git diff --staged --quiet || git commit -m "chore: deploy $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" git push git diff --staged --quiet exits 0 (no changes) → skip commit. Exits non-zero (changes present) → commit and push. The automated QA gate To catch these failures without manual checks, we added a verification step to the pipeline: Fetches the live site URL after a deploy Checks for the presence of the latest post title in the HTML Verifies the Last-Modified response header is newer than the previous deploy timestamp Fails the pipeline if either check doesn't pass This converts deployment verification from a manual check into an automated gate. Historical note: this postmortem covers the retired Hugo-based pipeline. The site has since moved to a direct-deploy model. ← All notes

pages.title: Registration Live: From Zero to Cloud Run in One Session — Notes
pages.description: How we took a broken multi-tenant registration build — Go backend, React frontend — to a live deployment on Google Cloud Run in a single engineering session.
headings: Registration Live: From Zero to Cloud Run in One Session
Starting point: five consecutive build failures
pages.text: Registration Live: From Zero to Cloud Run in One Session — Notes · Detroit Automation Academy Notes · DevOps · February 2026 Registration Live: From Zero to Cloud Run in One Session Published February 28, 2026 · Detroit Automation Academy · Historical engineering note — migrated from the retired blog. We shipped the academy registration system from a broken build to a fully deployed, publicly accessible system in a single engineering session. Here's what that actually looked like. Starting point: five consecutive build failures The deploy.sh script existed. The Docker images existed. What didn't exist: a working build. The first failure was a Go syntax error in backend/main.go — a raw newline embedded inside a string literal: // Broken fmt.Printf("Detroit Automation Academy Registration Backend starting on port %s... ", port) // Fixed fmt.Printf("...starting on port %s...\n", port) Go doesn't allow unescaped newlines inside string literals. The fix was one character. IAM permission cascade With the backend building, the push to Google Container Registry failed — the Compute service account had the right role but the Cloud Build service account didn't. We granted the missing role to both service accounts and the build cleared. The missing frontend scaffold The React frontend had App.tsx and EnrollmentForm.tsx — but no public/index.html , no src/index.tsx , and an invalid tsconfig.json . react-scripts build requires all three. We also caught a TypeScript error: inside an early-return block, TypeScript narrowed a view-state variable to a literal type, making a later comparison a dead branch (TS2367). Fixed by refactoring to a single return with conditional rendering. Replacing Terraform with direct deployment The deploy script ended with terraform init && terraform apply — but Terraform wasn't installed and the infra directory didn't exist. Rather than block, we replaced it with direct gcloud run deploy calls. Both backend and frontend were live in 60 seconds. Firestore persistence The original backend stored records in memory — wiped on every cold start. We rewrote the storage handler to use Firestore with a graceful in-memory fallback: Collections are tenant-namespaced If Firestore is unreachable, the handler falls back to thread-safe in-memory storage The /health endpoint reports which storage is active so you can tell at a glance Historical note: the endpoints from this session are no longer live. This post is preserved as an engineering record of the build. ← All notes

pages.title: Digital Stoicism: The Pause-and-Pivot Protocol — Notes
pages.description: Mastering the gap between a digital stimulus and your response: a 60-second firewall, a three-question audit, and the minimalist intervention.
pages.text: Digital Stoicism: The Pause-and-Pivot Protocol — Notes · Detroit Automation Academy Notes · Practice · February 2026 Digital Stoicism: The Pause-and-Pivot Protocol Published February 28, 2026 · Detroit Automation Academy · Historical note — migrated from the retired blog. In a digital environment designed for instant reaction, the most effective move is the intentional delay. This protocol is about emotional decoupling — separating a digital stressor from your immediate physical response. 1. The trigger You encounter a digital roadblock: an inflammatory comment, a confusing technical error, or a high-stakes misunderstanding in a group chat. Physical sign: increased heart rate, shallow breathing, or the urge to type fast. 2. The 60-second firewall Before your fingers touch the keys, implement a hard pause. Digital problems are often amplified by "hot" cognition. Moving to "cold" cognition allows for strategic rather than reactive solving. 3. The three-question audit Question Purpose Is this a bug or a feature? Determines if the problem is technical or intentional/human. What is my end goal? Shifts focus from "winning" to "resolving." Does this require a public or private response? Prevents escalation and preserves digital reputation. 4. The sage execution Once the minute is up, apply the minimalist intervention : Technical: search the error code + "solved." Interpersonal: use a neutral bridge statement — "I want to make sure I understand your point before I respond." The sage insight: responsibility in the digital age isn't about knowing every answer; it's about mastering the gap between a stimulus and your response. PAUSE & PIVOT SAGE PROTOCOL THE TRIGGER Urge to "Type Fast" or High Heart Rate ⏱️ 60s FIREWALL Move from Hot Reaction to Cold Strategy 1. Bug or Feature? Technical or Human Intentionality? 2. What is the Goal? Winning vs. Resolving 3. Public or Private? Reputation Preservation "Master the gap between stimulus and response." ← All notes

pages.title: The Ride Is Free — Detroit 2126 · The Signal
pages.description: Detroit 2126, installment one: the region voted to connect its transit system. What a century of fare-free, automated movement looks like — and the two-hour Detroit–Chicago link.
headings: Free works — and the receipts are in
Now the big one: Chicago in two hours
pages.text: The Ride Is Free — Detroit 2126 · The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Detroit 2126 · Installment 1 · September 2026 The Ride Is Free Published September 30, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn A new series. Same newsletter. The Signal has always covered the Detroiters building the future. This time we're asking a bigger question: what does Detroit look like in a hundred years if we build it for everyone who'll live here — not just everyone who can pay today? This series is called Detroit 2126. One city essential per installment. First up: how we move. The seeds are already planted On August 4, Wayne County did something this region has never done. Sixty-seven percent of voters — 230,387 people — approved a countywide transit millage. All 43 communities, including the 17 that had opted out of SMART, are in. Ten years of funding. In Detroit, the yes vote hit 85.8%. The millage authorizes up to 0.9831 mills — about 98 cents per $1,000 of taxable value, roughly $8 a month on a $100,000 home — through 2035. SMART's plan: eight new routes, five extensions, on-demand Flex service ($2–$8 a ride) where fixed routes don't make sense, phased through 2029. Next door in Oakland County, the 2022 millage produced a 49.5% ridership jump. The model works. And here's the part people forget: Detroit already runs one of America's few fully automated transit systems. The People Mover has been driverless since 1987 — thirteen stations, a downtown loop, a full circuit in about fifteen minutes. It's been zero-fare since 2024. Water Square station is mid-renovation, and an $800,000 system study is mapping two-way service, better stations, and three expansion corridors reaching Corktown, the Riverfront, and Eastern Market. The QLINE runs Woodward. DDOT runs the city buses, SMART the suburbs, and the RTA's Transit app puts all of them in one place with real-time arrivals and in-app fares. The pieces exist. They've just never been a system. On August 4, the region voted to change that. Free works — and the receipts are in This is where "free" stops being a fantasy. Two experiments ran it at scale, and the data came back. Luxembourg made all public transit free nationwide in 2020. In 2025, the national rail operator carried a record 31.4 million passengers. Luxembourg City's tram went from 6 million annual riders to over 31 million by 2024 — and kept growing. Kansas City went fare-free in 2020 too, the largest U.S. city to try it. A University of Kansas study published in Transport Policy found bus ridership 24% higher than peer cities, 17% of riders new to transit, and 92% saying they could shop for essentials and keep jobs they otherwise couldn't reach. Nearly 40% of existing riders rode more often. Riders without a car made nearly five more trips a week. Then the honest part: Kansas City reinstated fares in the summer of 2026, after six years, citing the money — about $18 million a year by 2025, growing. Free transit works. Funding it forever is the hard part. That's the 100-year question, right there. Not "can we afford free transit?" — Kansas City proved the ridership case — but "how do we fund it for a century?" Automation is part of the answer: the driverless loop downtown already runs without operator wages, and every mile of automated guideway pushes the per-ride cost closer to the floor. A fare is a tax on movement. Over a hundred years, the cities that tax movement the least will move the most. Now the big one: Chicago in two hours The Wolverine runs Detroit to Chicago three times a day each way — about 238 miles in five to six hours, at up to 110 mph on the Amtrak-owned stretch between Porter, Indiana and Kalamazoo. Michigan owns the 135 miles from Kalamazoo to Dearborn (bought from Norfolk Southern in 2012) and has been upgrading it toward 110. In fiscal 2025, Michigan's three state-supported routes carried a record 713,343 riders, with MDOT putting $20.2 million into operating support. Under the federal Corridor ID program, Michigan's plan is to double the Wolverine to six daily round trips, with a Detroit–Windsor extension on the table via the freight tunnel. A separate coast-to-coast study wraps in 2028. None of that is true high-speed rail — 110 mph is "higher-speed," and the honest number matters. But it's the foundation, and 231 of the 304 miles are publicly owned. The 100-year version: electrified, hourly, Detroit–Chicago in about two and a half hours, rolling into Michigan Central as the intermodal hub — regional rail on one level, the local transit network on the other. Ford's multimodal facility study is already underway. Imagine a century of that. The economic geography of the Midwest rewrites itself around a two-hour Detroit–Chicago link: commutes between the cities, supply chains that don't need a truck for the middle 300 miles, two downtowns functioning as one metro. The cities that built the interstate century won it. The cities that build the rail century win the next one. We built the prototype So we modeled it. The academy's 3D training district now runs the Forge Line: an elevated, automated guideway connecting five districts, modeled on the People Mover, with our training bot running microtransit underneath. Students don't just read about the reimagining. They drive it. Every real system started as a model someone could point at and argue with. Ours is live at detroitautomationacademy.com/#demo — go run the bot and tell us where the spokes should go. The work ahead The millage money starts flowing. The People Mover study lands. The corridors get drawn. The Wolverine doubles its frequencies. Somewhere in that process, the region decides whether "transit" means a bigger version of what we have — or something genuinely new. Our vote: build the thing that moves itself. The city that taught the world to drive can teach it to ride. And in a hundred years, nobody should have to pay for the privilege. The Signal is the newsletter of Detroit Automation Academy — where Detroit builds what's next. If you know a young builder who should be in the room, send them our way. pages.description: Detroit 2126, installment two: the median Detroit household earns $39,938; new builds list at $511,180. Who is it for? It's arithmetic.
pages.text: Who Is It For? — Detroit 2126 · The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Detroit 2126 · Installment 2 · October 2026 Who Is It For? Published October 5, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn Detroit 2126, part two. Last time: the ride is free. This time: the roof over your head. Here's the question, stated plainly, because it deserves no softening: why are we building unaffordable housing? Who is it for? The math Detroit's median household income is $39,938, per the Census Bureau. A third of the city lives in poverty. Now look at what's being built. Urban new-construction homes in the Detroit metro list at a median of $511,180 — a 176% premium over existing homes, per Realtor.com's March 2026 data. Zillow's July numbers tell the same story per square foot: $239 for new builds versus $165 for existing homes. And new construction is just 3.5% of sales, down from 4.4% in 2019. The standard rule of thumb says a household can afford a home worth about three times its income. A median Detroit household — $40,000 — can afford roughly $120,000. New builds are priced at more than four times that. At $301 a square foot (the median for new construction sold in the city proper between June 2025 and June 2026), a modest 1,200-square-foot house costs $361,000. That's nine times the median income. So: who is it for? It is not for the median Detroiter. That's not an accusation. It's arithmetic. The volume Between June 2025 and June 2026, exactly 19 new-construction homes sold in the entire city of Detroit, according to the Realtor MLS. Nineteen. The city holds some 50,000 vacant lots. Read that again. Fifty thousand empty lots. Nineteen new homes in a year. We are not experiencing a building boom that happens to be expensive. We are experiencing almost no building at all — and the little that gets built is priced for someone else. This is the shape of the problem: it's not that developers are flooding the market with luxury units. It's that the economics of building in Detroit barely work at any price point, so the only projects that clear the bar are the ones aimed at the top of it. Why Detroit housing developer David Palmer put it bluntly this summer: hard costs are the bulk of the bill, and there are few policy tools that touch them. Soft costs — permits, fees, approvals — are pure policy choices, and they can be lowered. But nobody has figured out how to make the actual sticks and bricks cheap enough to sell at $120,000. Then there's the appraisal gap: a rehabbed home often can't be valued high enough to serve as collateral for its own construction loan, because the comps around it are too low. The financing math breaks before the first nail is driven. And the buyers who do show up with money are increasingly not residents. A local realtor described watching young couples with clean FHA offers on $85,000 west-side bungalows lose to LLCs that wired cash and closed in days. They weren't beaten on price. They were beaten on speed — the one thing a financed buyer can't manufacture. Detroit's rent-to-value ratio is the second-highest in the country at 8.5%, which makes the city a magnet for independent investors: over 90% of the city's landlords own just one or two properties, accounting for 75% of the rental stock. Institutional buyers run only about 7% of metro purchases — this isn't Wall Street, it's thousands of small cash buyers, many from out of state, competing with residents for the same $85,000 bungalows and turning them into rentals. Meanwhile metro rents rose 1.7 to 3% in 2026 — leading the country — on a shortage that has persisted for decades. Waiting lists stretch through private rentals and assisted housing alike. So the honest answer to "who is it for": the new stuff is for the top of the market, because that's the only segment where the math closes. The existing stock is increasingly for investors, because cash beats a mortgage application. And the median household — $40,000 a year — is left bidding on what's left. The 100-year version Housing is the slowest-moving thing a city builds. A house framed today will shelter people in 2126, or it will be a vacant lot again by 2040. That makes it the purest 100-year question in this series. Here's what a century of building for everyone looks like. First, the cost problem gets attacked at the root: automated and modular construction — the academy's home territory — is the only lever big enough to move hard costs. We build the machines that build the things. A housing market that can't produce a $120,000 house is a robotics problem wearing a policy costume. Second, the land problem is already solved and sitting empty: 50,000 vacant lots, many held by the Land Bank, is one of the largest affordable-housing land assemblies in America. The question was never "where would we build." It's "who gets to build, and for whom." Third, the ownership model: community land trusts, limited-equity co-ops, and other structures that take land cost out of the price permanently — so a house built affordably in 2030 is still affordable in 2126, instead of flipping into the investor market the moment the neighborhood improves. None of this requires inventing a new Detroit. It requires deciding that the next hundred years of residents matter more than the next flip cycle. The work ahead Last installment, the region voted to connect its transit system. Housing needs its own version of that vote — not a millage, but a decision: that 50,000 lots become homes for the people who live here, built at prices the median household can actually pay. The ride is free. Now the roof. The Signal is the newsletter of Detroit Automation Academy — where Detroit builds what's next. The real story: the rulebook grew up
pages.text: BIOBUZZ Is Here: What the New FTC Season Demands — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Edition 1 · September 2026 BIOBUZZ Is Here: What the New FTC Season Demands Published September 23, 2026 · Read on LinkedIn The 2026-27 FIRST Tech Challenge season kicked off on September 12, and the game is BIOBUZZ. The theme is pollination. The challenge is precision. And the rulebook just changed how it wants to be read. Here's what matters, in plain language. The game Two alliances, two teams each. Forty yellow POLLEN balls and sixteen alliance-colored NECTAR balls. Three scoring structures: The HIVE sits at field center. Each alliance has a two-chambered hive on a pivot. Launch scoring elements into the upward-facing chamber, and when enough weight lands, it tips — 20 points per tip. Every tip also unlocks one more NECTAR from your staging area. Your launcher is your season. The FLOWERS hang on the walls, and they only score in the last 60 seconds. Load them from the top. Here's the twist: whoever's NECTAR sits top-most owns the flower — and the owner scores 2 points for every element inside, no matter who put it there. The final minute isn't an endgame. It's the whole match, compressed. The GARDENS in the corners pay 1 point per element, but they're unprotected. Anything you leave there can be stolen. Matches run 30 seconds of autonomous, an 8-second transition, then 2 minutes driver-controlled. The rule changes worth coaching Four elements, that's it. Robots can control at most four scoring elements at once, and hoarding to deny opponents is its own major foul. Cycle speed beats stockpiling this year. Let it land. When a hive tips, spilled elements must hit the floor before anyone collects them. No camping under the hive with an open intake. Flowers are gated. NECTAR entering a flower before the last 60 seconds is a major foul per element . Practice the endgame as an endgame. One legal way to tip a hive: launching into the upward chamber. Ramming the frame is a foul. The human player is a real position now. NECTAR enters one-per-tip, or all-remaining under 60 seconds, only through the loading zone, no tools. Train that person. Autonomous pays: leave the wall (3), park (5), tip a hive (20) — and 16 combined leave-and-park points across the alliance earns a ranking point. Robot constraints, for the builders: start inside an 18-inch cube, expand to 18x24x29, no weight limit, max 8 motors and 8 servos. The real story: the rulebook grew up Buried in section 1.4.1 is the season's biggest change, and it isn't a game mechanic. FIRST rewrote the manual's philosophy: rules now emphasize the spirit of the rule and the intended gameplay, and event volunteers are empowered to make good-faith judgment calls instead of logging every incident. That's a bet on human judgment over legalism — and it changes how every team should read every rule this season. Don't hunt loopholes. Ask what the rule is protecting, and build for that. We'll be coaching it as a habit, not a footnote. What we're doing about it Our fall cohort isn't rebuilding season prep from scratch. We've turned the manual into a starter kit: the rule changes that matter, eight targeted drills (launcher accuracy, spill recovery, the 60-second flower sprint, possession discipline, autonomous routines), and a four-week practice plan that ends in full scrimmages with refs calling the real fouls. Month one is about three things: a launcher that tips hives, an autonomous routine that banks points, and an endgame that wins the last minute. pages.text: BIOBUZZ, Week Two: The Three Bets That Win This Season — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Edition 2 · September 2026 BIOBUZZ, Week Two: The Three Bets That Win This Season Published September 25, 2026 · Read on LinkedIn The game reveal was two weeks ago. Kickoff watch parties are over. The whiteboards are full, the field kits are arriving, and teams across the world are making the first irreversible decisions of their season — what to build first, what to practice, where to bet their limited build hours. Here is the coach's read on the three bets that will decide BIOBUZZ. The season is real now More than 120,000 students worldwide are expected to take part in this season's FIRST Tech Challenge, which FIRST is calling BIOBUZZ presented by RTX — part of the 2026–27 FIRST CANOPY season. The biodiversity theme is pollination. The field is built around it: pollen, nectar, hives, flowers, gardens. Kickoff events drew teams together to stream the reveal and tear the game apart in real time. Registration is open and qualifying tournaments are already on the calendar — league play starts as early as November in some regions. The clock is running. Bet #1: The launcher wins this season Every hive tip is 20 points, and the only legal way to tip a hive is launching into the upward-facing chamber. Ram the frame and you'll draw a warning — do it to gain an edge and it's a major foul. Camp under the hive with an open intake and the refs will warn you — spilled elements have to hit the floor first. So the launcher is not one subsystem among many. It is the season's bottleneck. An accurate launcher tips hives; hives tip matches. Everything else — drivetrain, intake, lift — exists to feed the launcher or defend against someone else's. The practical question for every team: can your launcher hit the upward chamber from across the field, repeatedly, under defense? If the answer is yes, you have a robot worth building around. If not, nothing downstream matters yet. Bet #2: The last 60 seconds are the whole match The flowers hang on the walls and only score in the final minute. Load them from the top. Whoever's nectar sits top-most owns the flower — and the owner scores 2 points for every element inside, no matter who put it there. That mechanic flips endgame strategy on its head. A flower stuffed with pollen is not a points bank; it is a prize waiting for a new owner. The final minute is not an endgame. It is the whole match, compressed — a sprint for flower ownership where positioning beats accumulation. And the entry gates hard: nectar entering a flower before the last 60 seconds is a major foul per element. Practice the endgame as an endgame. Bet #3: The human player is a real position One detail keeps getting underrated. Nectar enters the field one-per-hive-tip — or all-remaining under 60 seconds — only through the loading zone, and the human player may use no tools. That person feeds every piece of nectar your robot will ever score. Human players used to be whoever wasn't driving. This season, the position has mechanics worth training: feeding under pressure, cycling quickly and cleanly, reading the field while the driver reads the robot. Treat it like a position — reps, drills, and a named person who owns it — and it becomes an edge. Treat it as an afterthought and every possession starts behind. What week-one whiteboards look like River City Robotics, an Edmonton-area program, published their week-one whiteboard — and it's representative of what good week-one thinking looks like: a drivetrain that's quick and doesn't mind getting bumped, an intake that scoops both ball sizes off the floor, a launcher accurate enough to hit the hive cell from across the field, a camera reading the AprilTags under the hive so the robot knows which way it tipped, and an autonomous routine that launches the four preloaded pollen, leaves the wall, and parks. Notice the shape of that list. Launcher accuracy. Floor-level intake. Orientation sensing. Autonomous banking. None of it is exotic — it is the fundamentals, aimed at the three bets. What we're doing about it Our fall cohort is in week two of the four-week practice plan: launcher tuning and spill recovery this week, flower sprint drills next, then full scrimmages with refs calling the real fouls. Month one is about three things — a launcher that tips hives, an autonomous routine that banks points, and an endgame that wins the last minute. Everything else can wait. pages.text: The Rulebook Changed Again — and the Robots Keep Moving to Detroit — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Edition 4 · October 2026 The Rulebook Changed Again — and the Robots Keep Moving to Detroit Published October 5, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn Three weeks into BIOBUZZ, the rulebook has already changed twice. Team Update 01 landed September 17 — a hive-height correction (the bottom of the hive sits 30.6 inches above the tiles), a yellow/red card cleanup, and a clarified Question Box process: technical questions go to the FTA, and up to two student reps talk to the head ref after match results post. Team Update 02 landed September 24, and this one changes how you play. The current manual is version TU02. If your strategy doc still says TU01, update it. Defense has a bright line now G420 — "do not tip or entangle" — got examples that matter. Contact with exposed wiring or a fragile intake in normal play: probably not a violation. Using a wedge to tip an opponent: strategic. Slamming frame-to-frame into a robot that's trying to right itself: strategic. Touching a robot that has already started tipping, if the ref decides you could have avoided it: strategic. And "strategic" is the expensive word in this year's manual. It turns warnings into majors and majors into yellow and red cards. The season's new Competition Integrity Contract plus the defined STRATEGIC term means refs are told to judge intent, not just geometry. So practice your defense driving against that standard. If your driver can't tell you where the line is — the moment contact becomes a card — they'll find it in a qualification match, and it will cost your alliance. The human player can bank nectar G426 was rewritten around two words: "whichever comes first." Nectar enters when a hive tips, or when the clock hits 60 seconds — and your human player is not required to feed nectar the instant a hive tips. They can hold it. The primary field timer is the cue. And refs want the remaining nectar kept visible and unambiguous in the alliance area, so there's no question about what's waiting. That turns the human player into a tactician. Edition 2 called the human player a real position. TU02 upgraded the job description: timing the nectar dump is now a decision, not a reflex. Bank your nectar, flood the last minute, take the flowers. One more date: the official Team Q&A opened September 28. When your drivers hit a gray area in TU02, ask it there — answers from the Q&A system carry weight at events. The robots are moving to Detroit This month, Danish autonomous mobile robot maker Robotize announced its first U.S. office — in metro Detroit. Their GoPal pallet-transport robots already had customers and partners on this side of the Atlantic; now the company has a home here too, led by 25-year industry veteran Dan Hasley. They're not the only ones. Teradyne Robotics — the group behind Universal Robots and MiR — is standing up its U.S. operations hub in Wixom this year: building UR cobots here, plus a training, service, and visitor center with more than 200 jobs behind it. Two global robotics companies planting flags in metro Detroit in one year. That's not a coincidence; it's a verdict. The work is coming here. The question is who gets to do it — and that is the entire argument for a pipeline that starts with a seventh grader and a robot kit. Manufacturing Day was Friday MFG Day is the first Friday of October, every year — this year, October 2. Factories across the country opened their doors. If you know a young person who's never stood on a production floor, mark October 1, 2027 now. And the new Detroit 2126 series launched with installment one, "The Ride Is Free," on fare-free transit and the future of Detroit–Chicago rail. We're at 32 subscribers. The flywheel is turning. pages.text: Every Stop, Counted — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Edition 5 · October 2026 Every Stop, Counted Published October 15, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn Detroit's transit map got honest this month — about what it shows, and about what it still can't. The QLINE is on the map — on its own tracks The streetcar joined Live Transit Detroit on October 14, built from the QLINE's own published GTFS: all 12 stations, the Grand Boulevard terminus, and the downtown terminal loop, with live positions from the QLINE's public real-time feed. Getting there took three fixes, each found the same way — by checking the map against the street: a sign error that mirrored the track miles from where it belonged, a street centerline standing in for the actual track alignment, and a rendering cap written for a smaller map that silently clipped stops. The full story is Live Transit Detroit installment six, "The QLINE Sign Error." 10,583 stops, rebuilt from source The launch completed a full rebuild of the map's stop registry from the agencies' own GTFS data: 5,124 DDOT stops, 5,437 SMART stops, and 22 QLINE stops — the QLINE previously had none. Every production stop ID was preserved, so nothing that referenced a stop before the rebuild broke after it. The count is verifiable the same way everything on the map is: go look. The honest part SMART's live feed still waits on SMART. The schedules are not the obstacle — all 45 SMART routes and all 5,437 SMART stops are on the map. What's missing is the real-time key, which runs through SMART's approval at Swiftly. Our October inquiry drew an automated acknowledgment and, so far, no answer; a formal key request followed on October 13. Until it lands, SMART positions arrive through a fallback that was never live, and the map's job is to say so rather than dress it up. We published the full account as a press release on October 14 — it's on the site, and it's the standing offer: the day the key arrives, SMART goes live on the same 60-second cadence as everything else. As of tonight the map labels the fallback for what it is: "SMART positions as of 10:40 PM — snapshot, not live GPS," with the count itself marked stale once a snapshot passes an hour old. What's next Two builds that were next are live. Service alerts shipped on October 14: DDOT bulletins and SMART notices as badges on the routes they affect, an active-alerts list, and the effects in plain language — 32 bulletins were active the night it shipped. And the trip planner's timing model was audited against the buses' own reported departures: at terminal stops it had been adding dwell that never happened, 806 seconds of phantom wait in the worst timing cells. Corrected, those cells read 269 seconds, against a 322-second clean baseline. What is actually next is the events layer — concerts, games, and festivals as destinations the trip planner understands, appearing only while they're relevant. Its sources are settled: Ticketmaster, the league feed for Red Wings games, and Eastern Market, with the major annual festivals entered by hand once their dates are confirmed. Thirty-four subscribers got the first transit edition. This one goes to whoever's joined since. The work is the pitch: every stop, counted — and every gap, labeled. pages.text: What the Pictures Say Now — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Special Edition · October 2026 What the Pictures Say Now Published October 5, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn Published off-cycle. Some weeks the build is concrete; this week it's words. The University of Michigan's Disability Equity Office is running a 10-Week Accessibility Challenge, and this week's theme is alt text — the short descriptions that let screen readers speak images aloud. The premise is simple: people who are blind or have low vision navigate the web with screen readers, and when a screen reader reaches an image, it reads the alt text. No alt text, no image. Bad alt text, a bad image. We decided to stop theorizing and audit the whole site. Every page on detroitautomationacademy.com, every image: 50 images across 16 pages, each one opened and looked at before a word was written. What we found was unflattering in the specific way these audits always are. Thirty of the fifty were our own logo sitting next to the written-out name "Detroit Automation Academy" — the digital equivalent of introducing yourself twice. Four were CAD renders of the Forge Line vehicles whose alt text repeated the card heading word for word. Seven were Signal cover artworks labeled, with great precision, "cover art." All of it is fixed now. The logos are marked decorative, so screen readers skip them instead of announcing the academy's name twice per page. The vehicle renders describe what you'd actually see — "boxy orange passenger railcar with a dark window band" — because the heading already tells you its name. The covers describe their artwork: the steampunk pollen launcher on Edition 4, the wood-framed house glowing under construction on the Detroit 2126 housing installment, the ballot and magnifying glass under the Forge D on the voter-guide edition. The standard we applied, straight from the challenge guide: be concise, describe what's essential in context, never restate the caption, never write "image of," and mark the purely decorative as decorative. Two images were already correct and untouched — the big hero mark on the homepage, and an animation-frame graphic that was already hidden from assistive tech. One honest footnote from the guide, worth repeating: AI tools keep getting better at identifying what's in a picture, but alt text conveys information in context , and that still needs human judgment. These descriptions were drafted with AI assistance, then checked against each image and its surrounding page before anything went live. That's the whole point of the exercise. This is week two of ten for us. There's more of the challenge ahead — and if you navigate with a screen reader and hit a barrier anywhere on the site, we want to hear about it . That's not a slogan; it's a bug report we haven't received yet. Cover photo: braille terminal photo by Sebastien.delorme , CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. headings: Thirty Days to Keep the Doors Open
pages.text: Thirty Days to Keep the Doors Open — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Special Edition · September 2026 Thirty Days to Keep the Doors Open Published September 29, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn Published off-cycle. The timeline here is measured in days, not months. On Woodward Avenue in the North End sits a 15,000-square-foot grocery store that keeps having to explain what it is. The Detroit People's Food Co-op opened in early 2024 as Detroit's first Black-led grocery store — community-owned, built around fresh, healthy, local food at reasonable prices. This week it made its situation public: a fundraising push to keep the doors open, with about a month on the clock. The numbers underneath are worth sitting with. The co-op does roughly $3 million in annual sales. It pays solid wages. Much of its stock is priced in line with, or below, the big chains. And still it is struggling — against rising food costs, against half a year without a full-time general manager (the search took six months; the manager they found was then in an accident and has only recently returned part-time), and against something no amount of revenue fixes on its own: people don't understand the model. Malik Yakini, who has helped lead the project from the start, is direct about it. Some neighbors mistake the store for a food pantry. Others assume you need a membership to shop, "like at Sam's Club." Neither is true. Anyone can walk in and buy food — no membership, no extra charge. Membership, open to anyone 21 or older for a small fee, is something else entirely: ownership. A vote. A committee seat. A share of the profits, if there are any. That distinction is the whole point, and Yakini says it better than anyone: "Clearly it is more than a grocery store, and the value proposition is much larger in terms of community development, creating community based jobs, and creating a democratic institution that is owned by community members." Why this is in The Signal: we usually write about Detroiters building the future with machines. But sometimes the future is an institution — a store that keeps money in Detroit instead of sending it to out-of-town chains, that trains Black Detroiters in grocery management in a city where roughly eighty stores offer almost no such path, that answers to its neighbors instead of distant shareholders. That is infrastructure too. The ask is concrete, and it is time-boxed. Three ways in: Donate. The co-op's Mframadan campaign — "a house built to withstand windy and treacherous conditions" — is live on GoFundMe through November 30: gofundme.com/f/support-detroit-peoples-food-coops-urgent-needs Invest. $1,000 minimum, repaid over several years with negotiated interest. Write to invest@detroitpeoplesfoodcoop.com . Show up. Become a member-owner — or just go shop there. The store is open daily, 8am to 8pm, and the shelves need customers as much as the campaign needs dollars. The co-op is resetting its in-store operations — "to make sure that when people come in they're having a good experience," Yakini says — and taking its case to churches, community groups, fraternities and sororities across the city. Thirty days is not much time. But against roughly $3 million in annual sales, it's a bridge. pages.text: Every DDOT Bus, Live, in 3D — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Special Edition · October 2026 Every DDOT Bus, Live, in 3D Published October 5, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn Tonight we're opening the beta on something we've been building for weeks: a live 3D map of every DDOT bus route in Detroit — all 37 routes, drawn as elevated guideways over the actual streets, with real bus positions updating every 60 seconds. It's here: detroitautomationacademy.com/live-transit.html And as of this week, it's not just a map anymore. Hit Plan trip and it becomes a navigator. What you're looking at Thirty-seven colored routes across the whole city — the ten ConnectTen crosstown routes, the primary corridors like Woodward and Michigan Avenue, and seventeen neighborhood routes — with 5,120 stops plotted along them. Every glowing pillar on the map is a real bus, reporting its position right now. Filter the map by group or by individual route. Click any bus and you'll get its vehicle number, the actual model (New Flyer XD40, XD60 articulated, Proterra electric — real fleet data), seating, speed, and heading. Zoom in close and the pillars resolve into true-scale bus bodies: a 40-foot bus rendered at a real 40 feet. Zoom out and you're looking at the whole system at once. Routes with no buses out get out of the way on their own — they dim or hide automatically, and the filter panel tells you exactly how many routes are currently running. Plan a trip, with live delays The new Plan trip button runs a real trip planner (RAPTOR, the same algorithm family behind professional transit apps) on DDOT's actual schedule data — up to 3 itineraries, transfers included, drawn on the map as elevated guideways with a cinematic fly-through. Here's the part we're proudest of: the planner watches the live buses. When a bus is matched to your trip, the times shift to reflect reality — a +8 min late badge on the leg, a data-age label ("live 45s old") so you know how fresh the reading is. If the bus is too far off schedule to trust, the leg gets flagged disrupted instead of showing you a fiction. And while you ride, the page guides you: board-soon alerts, alight-next callouts, and automatic replanning if a live delay costs you a transfer. No account. No app install. Your origin and destination never leave your device. The honest engineering Positions come from DDOT's live vehicle feed, polled every 60 seconds and batched so the entire system costs four upstream requests a minute — the map will not get our API access revoked. Every position is also logged to a public dataset every five minutes, so the map paints instantly from the last logged positions while the live feed connects. Schedules come from DDOT's GTFS feed, and the delay layer is pure measurement: we match each live bus to its scheduled trip by position, stop sequence, and headsign, then shift only the remaining stop times by the measured delay — clamped, smoothed across polls, and dropped entirely if the bus goes quiet. When the observed data isn't good enough to stand behind, the page says so instead of guessing. Behind the scenes, every five minutes of observations feeds an empirical timing model — real segment-by-segment travel times, built from the buses themselves. Once a segment has enough observations, the planner will start preferring measured reality over the printed schedule. No deploy needed; the page just gets smarter. This is a beta — break it Open beta means we want your eyes on it. The most useful thing you can tell us: where the map disagrees with the street. A route drawn wrong, a bus that looks off its route, a stop in the wrong place — that's the feedback that makes it better. New this week: tell us where the planner disagrees with reality. A delay badge that looks wrong, a transfer it should have caught, a trip that doesn't match what you rode — that's the feedback that trains the system. Send it all to dbkr@umich.edu — a screenshot and the route number is plenty. Why we're building this In April, Detroit made every DDOT bus free for K–12 students. Show a school ID, ride anywhere the bus goes — no pass, no paperwork. The program is called Ride to Rise; it launched as a six-month pilot and now runs through the 2026–27 school year on $1 million in state funding. The city reported 44,000 student rides in the first month of the school year. SMART did the same for students across three counties in May — K–12 through college, no end date. Free is the fare. The missing piece is navigation. A student who has never ridden the bus doesn't need a timetable — they need to see the system. Which bus. Which direction. Whether it's actually coming. That's what this page is for: the map a first-time rider can read at a glance, with live buses, direction arrows, and the destination on every bus. This is the academy's thesis in one page: real city data, rendered honestly, built in Detroit — in service of the kids who just got the keys to the system. The same feed powers a youth data-science module we're developing: students working with the same live buses they're riding. The pipeline starts with a seventh grader and a dataset. pages.title: Shut Down by the Meter — The Signal
pages.description: A Signal special edition: on October 15, 2026, Netlify quota-paused the hosted service behind Live Transit Detroit's live data — HTTP 503 usage_exceeded on every endpoint — and DDOT's BusTime key hit its daily cap the same day. What was shut down, why, what the service had already proven, and where it stands now.
headings: What was shut down — and what was not
The day's second budget: DDOT's transaction cap
What the service had already proven
pages.text: Shut Down by the Meter — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Special Edition · October 2026 Shut Down by the Meter Published October 15, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn Published off-cycle, on the day of the events it records. On October 15, 2026, at approximately 3:24 PM Eastern, the hosted service behind Live Transit Detroit's live data stopped answering. Every path on the proxy — /healthz , /api/vehicles , /api/alerts , and the site root — returned HTTP 503 with the body {"error":"usage_exceeded"} . The host, Netlify, had quota-paused the site. The live feed was down for every visitor until it was rebuilt later the same afternoon. This special edition records what was shut down, why the meter ran out, what the service had already proven by the day it closed, and where things stand now. What was shut down — and what was not What was shut down is specific: the hosted live-data proxy and the public API endpoints it served. The Live Transit page drew its entire live layer — vehicle positions and service alerts — from that proxy, so at the pause the map stopped receiving live data. Everything else that lived on the same host went down with it, including the five-minute telemetry logger described below. What was not shut down: this website and the Live Transit map itself. They are hosted on GitHub Pages, a separate system that was unaffected throughout. The site never closed, no page was removed, and the map's stops, routes, geometry, and journey planner — all of which run on published data served with the site — remained available. The shutdown was a data-service shutdown, not a site closure, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Why: the meter The proxy ran on Netlify's Personal plan: $9 per month, upgraded on October 10, carrying a budget of 1,000 credits per month. Credits are consumed by the hosted work the site performs. Three standing loads drew against that budget continuously. First, the page itself: every open copy of the Live Transit page polled two proxy endpoints — vehicles every 60 seconds, alerts every 120 seconds — so proxy invocations scaled with the audience. Second, the telemetry logger: a scheduled function on the same Netlify site polled the same upstreams every five minutes and appended vehicle records to the transit-data archive that the empirical timing model is built from. Third, our own verification traffic, which was heavy that day. At approximately 3:24 PM the budget was exhausted and the host paused the site outright — not a degraded mode, a hard stop on every path. The architectural contribution is ours and is stated plainly: the proxy design called its upstreams in response to page traffic, so its cost grew with the number of people using the map. A public service whose cost scales with its audience, running on a fixed monthly meter, has a known failure date; the only unknown is which day it lands on. It landed on October 15. The telemetry stream's fate is the same lesson in a second form. Because the logger shared the host, it shared the pause: the JSONL event stream, the timing-model inputs, and the page's history overlay froze at the same moment. The logger was repointed to the rebuilt feed the same afternoon; its stream records the interruption as a bounded gap of 32 minutes 5 seconds, represented as a gap and never backfilled. The day's second budget: DDOT's transaction cap The same day carried a second, independent budget failure, upstream of us. DDOT's BusTime API — the source of DDOT vehicle positions and service bulletins — documents a default limit of 10,000 requests per day per key (Clever Devices, BusTime Developer API Guide , v3, §1.5). On October 15 the key returned the error "Transaction limit for current day has been exceeded," recorded in our own alerts file at 20:15 UTC. DDOT vehicles had read as zero from approximately 1:12 PM Eastern. The cause connects directly to the design retired that day. Until October 15, the key's consumer was the same per-page-view proxy: it ran a 41-call pattern — 4 batched vehicle calls and 37 per-route bulletin calls — on every page-driven poll, so daily volume scaled with audience and reached the cap by early afternoon. The rebuilt feed is fixed-cadence by construction: one builder, one schedule, and a volume that does not grow with the audience. Even so, the arithmetic had to be faced honestly — 41 calls across 288 five-minute cycles is approximately 11,800 transactions per day, above the documented default on its own. Bulletin collection was therefore moved to an hourly sub-cadence, bringing the operating volume to approximately 2,040 transactions per day, inside the default cap. A request to raise the cap — to 50,000 transactions per day, with 25,000 stated as acceptable — was sent to DDOT on October 15 and is now in DDOT's hands. DDOT live positions return with the provider's daily reset; the durable arrangement depends on that decision. What the service had already proven The shutdown arrived one day after the Live Transit Detroit series published a case study of the map's native journey planner, and the results stand independent of the hosting failure. The reference journey runs from Providence Hospital to Woodward & Warren, ready at 12:45 PM on a Thursday, computed entirely from DDOT's published schedule. The native optimum is the three-bus sequence 10-3-8: 57 minutes, arriving 1:42 PM. Measured against the same ready time, the fastest answers from the three external engines benchmarked — Google Maps, the DDOT trip planner, and Moovit — were all built on SMART buses and arrived at 1:55 PM, 1:59 PM, and 2:01 PM respectively. DDOT route 3, the middle leg of the native optimum, appears in zero of the 25 itineraries those engines returned. Engine Fastest routing Arrival Live Transit Detroit (native, DDOT only) DDOT 10 → 3 → 8 1:42 PM Google Maps SMART 710 → 462 1:55 PM DDOT trip planner SMART 710 → 462 1:59 PM Moovit SMART 710 → 462/461 2:01 PM The study behind the headline is larger than one trip. Across 259 departures spanning Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday service, the two-transfer winner's advantage decomposes exactly: the third bus does not add ride cost — its ride-and-walk component was lower in 259 of 259 instances — it relocates the wait to a faster connection. A generalization census then re-optimized 630 journeys (15 hub nodes, all 210 directed pairs, three departures) and measured every leg of every optimum by removing it and re-planning: 752 of 1,083 legs in optimal journeys are load-bearing at a margin of five minutes or more. Two-transfer optima hold 189 of those 752 load-bearing legs — 25.1 percent of them. The visibility result is the finding with a boundary, and the boundary is part of the result. In the demonstration phase, external engines offered the exact native sequence in 7 of 8 instances — at rank 1 every time it was offered — whenever the optimum was direct or single-transfer. Two-transfer optima were surfaced in 0 of 5 engine measurements. The invisible class is the multi-transfer optimum whose connecting middle leg — route 3 in the Providence journey, route 31 in one demonstration instance — an engine must specifically construct. The Providence invisibility was real; the generalization phase establishes it as a property of that journey class, not of native computation generally. Where things stand now The product is DDOT and QLINE. SMART was removed from the map the same day (build 20261015-1502), a priority decision recorded in the Live Transit Detroit series' files: the map now carries all 37 DDOT routes and 5,124 DDOT stops, and the QLINE streetcar. The QLINE streetcar remains fully live on the map in the interim. Its positions never depended on the shut-down host or on the DDOT key — the QLINE feed is a public GTFS-Realtime stream the rebuilt builder reads directly — and at last verification the feed carried 4 streetcars with current positions on the Woodward corridor. While DDOT live positions are dark, users are free to enjoy the QLINE in the interim: it is running, it is on the map, and it is live in the same sense it has always been. The feed itself was rebuilt the same afternoon on infrastructure the Academy runs itself. A workflow in this site's own repository polls the upstreams every five minutes and publishes the live data as static files on the site; the page reads those files, and a small dispatch driver on our own machine holds the five-minute cadence after GitHub's scheduler fired zero scheduled runs on the first day. The telemetry stream was repointed to the same feed. A service degradation notice is also live on the page (build 20261015-1638): when a data source degrades, the page now states which source, since when, and what still works, instead of presenting silence as if it were an empty street. The public API documentation page records the retired proxy endpoints as retired, with the reason. What remains open is DDOT live positions. As of publication they await the provider's daily reset, and the durable fix is the cap decision described above. Nothing in the current state is fabricated to cover that gap: the DDOT leg of the feed reports its actual state, and the map shows DDOT's scheduled service — every stop, every route, the planner — while the live layer is dark. The close The hosted public API that other tools and pages could call is retired, and this special edition is its record. We hope to be back in the future — with fuller live coverage than the map carries today — when the data arrangements allow it. That is stated as hope and intent, not as a promise and not with a date: the two failures recorded here were both, at bottom, arrangements that did not hold, and the next arrangement will be announced when it exists, not before. In the meantime the map is open, the planner is computing, the streetcar is live, and the work continues on infrastructure we run ourselves. pages.title: The Trip Your App Doesn't Show You — The Signal
pages.description: A Signal special edition in plain language: when Detroit's fastest bus journey takes two transfers, the big apps usually don't show it at all. Of 24 best two-transfer journeys tested, Google showed 2 and Moovit showed 5 — while both showed 7 of 8 one-transfer journeys.
headings: The Trip Your App Doesn't Show You
The home team does its own math
pages.text: The Trip Your App Doesn't Show You — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Special Edition · October 2026 The Trip Your App Doesn't Show You Published October 16, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn The study behind the map, in plain language. The fastest bus trip from Providence Hospital to Woodward & Warren arrives at 1:42 PM. Google never showed it. Moovit never showed it — not first, not fifth, not anywhere on the list. Three buses: the 10, the 3, the 8. Leave at 12:45, arrive at 1:42. Google's best answer got there at 1:55. Moovit's at 2:01. And route 3 — the middle bus, the one that makes the whole trip work — appeared in none of the 25 itineraries the outside planners returned between them. One trip could be a fluke. So we tested it properly. First, the rules We wrote the plan before we ran a single check. Every trip picked by rule, not by us. No cherry-picking after seeing the answers. We built every best journey we could construct among 15 key places — transit centers, busy corners, a hospital, campuses. 630 journeys. 88 of them needed two transfers. A fixed rule picked 24 of those 88 to test. For comparison, we added 8 best journeys needing only one transfer, matched as closely as we could. Then we asked Google and Moovit for every trip, at the exact day and time the plan called for. 64 checks in all. The score Of the 24 best two-transfer journeys, Google showed 2. Moovit showed 5. Scale that up to all 88, and the best estimate is stark: about 89 of every 100 of these journeys are invisible to Google. About 78 of every 100 are invisible to Moovit. The test group is small, so here is the honest range, not just the headline. Google's true figure sits somewhere between about 56 and 97 of 100. Moovit's, between about 44 and 94. At minimum: more than half of these trips go unseen. At best estimate: the large majority. One transfer? No problem Now give the same apps a journey with one transfer. Two buses, one change. Both showed 7 of 8. Same apps. Same city. Same test. The failures are not random. They pile up exactly where a journey needs two transfers. Blame the middle bus Look at which trips went missing. Some have a middle bus doing the real work: take it out of the network and the trip falls apart, or gets much slower. Others have a middle bus you could delete for free. Google showed none of the first kind. Not one of 14. Its only two hits were the free-to-delete kind — and even those showed up only on trips arriving 27 and 28 minutes later than the best one. The rider never knows Picture the rider. No car. Phone in hand. She asks the app how to get across town. If the fastest trip needs two transfers, chances are the app never shows it. She is not offered a slightly worse trip. The trip itself is hidden — and she never learns it existed. She just concludes the bus takes forever. Or doesn't go there at all. For a rider who depends on the bus, that is the difference between a city that works and a city that doesn't. Checked, re-checked, reviewed We wrote the plan before testing. We picked every trip by rule. When a few early checks turned out to have run at the wrong time or the wrong day, we threw them out and ran them again. Two re-runs changed answers in the apps' favor — those are the answers in the results. Then three reviewers who had no part in the study re-checked every number in it. The home team does its own math Detroit's own planner — built into the Live Transit Detroit map on this site — does its own math, straight from the bus schedules. Google's answers and Moovit's answers are never fed into it. It found the 1:42 trip because it read the timetable, not the apps. The full technical record — every trip, every number, every method — is Installment 07 of Live Transit Detroit, "The Invisible Middle Leg." pages.title: The Triumphant Return — The Signal
pages.description: A Signal special edition: on October 15, 2026, SMART returned to Live Transit Detroit the same day it was removed — 5,437 stops restored to a 10,583-stop registry, 83 routes, on a licensed Swiftly feed at 1.7 percent of its limit — and was uplifted from beta to full production that night. With a public thank-you to Dante' of Swiftly Technical Support.
headings: How it came back: a key, a license, and terms first
pages.text: The Triumphant Return — The Signal · Detroit Automation Academy The Signal · Special Edition · October 2026 The Triumphant Return Published October 16, 2026 · By Justin Spencer Smith · Also on LinkedIn Published off-cycle, on the day the map became whole again. On October 15, 2026, The Signal published a special edition titled "Shut Down by the Meter." It closed with a hope, stated carefully: to be back in the future with fuller live coverage, when the data arrangements allowed it. That was stated as hope and intent — not as a promise, and not with a date. The return began the same day. This special edition records it. What came back SMART is back on Live Transit Detroit — all of it. On the afternoon of October 15, SMART had been removed from the map: its segment of the stop registry was tombstoned, set aside rather than deleted, in a removal built to be reversible. That evening the segment was restored at its original positions: 5,437 SMART stops returned, bringing the registry back to 10,583 stops and the map back to 83 routes — 37 DDOT, 45 SMART, and the QLINE streetcar. Because the removal had been designed for reversal, the return was a restoration, not a rebuild, and it could happen in hours instead of weeks. How it came back: a key, a license, and terms first The shutdown had two causes: the hosted proxy behind the live data exhausted its host's meter, and DDOT's BusTime key hit its daily transaction cap. SMART's return runs on a different arrangement entirely. Swiftly, the transit data platform, issued the Academy an API key for SMART data on October 15 (agency key detroit-smartbus ), covering GTFS-Realtime vehicle positions and trip updates, with a usage limit of 180 requests per 15 minutes. The draw against that limit is deliberately small. The rebuilt feed reads Swiftly on a fixed five-minute cadence — about 12 requests per hour, roughly 1.7 percent of the issued limit — and the volume does not grow with the audience. That is the lesson of the meter, applied. The license posture is display-only, and it is structural rather than promised. Under the license's terms (§4(vi)), SMART vehicles render on the map from a separate display payload; they are never merged into the public vehicles feed, and the telemetry archive excludes SMART records by construction. Both separations were proven with live data on the day of the return. And before a single SMART bus reappeared, the end-user terms the license requires were published on the site (build 20261015-1919). SMART was reactivated that evening on those terms (build 20261015-2034) — with SMART enabled, the evening's verification counted 114 live vehicles on the map. From beta to production For its first hours back, SMART returned under its pre-removal treatment: a filter group labeled "SMART (beta)", off by default, with each visitor's choice remembered. That night it was uplifted to full production (build 20261015-2249). The group is now labeled simply "SMART" and is on by default, like DDOT and QLINE; a visitor who has chosen otherwise keeps their choice — the stored preference wins over the default. Beta was the right posture for a feed of uncertain standing. The Swiftly arrangement is licensed, metered at a fraction of its limit, and verified; production is the right posture for that. Verified the same night The return was audited the night it happened. A two-pass UAT fidelity audit compared the production map against the approved state of the nine items shipped across this build-out — the home framing, route naming, camera memory, the planner service-day fix, the app-lock fix, the feed migration, the service degradation notice, the end-user terms, and the SMART reactivation itself. Static fidelity first, then interactive checks on the live page. The result: every item measured as approved, with zero unexplained divergences. A return that is verified is a return that can be announced, and this one was. A thank-you, by name One person made the same-day return possible, and he should be named in the same public way the shutdown was. Dante' of Swiftly Technical Support issued the Academy's key on October 15 — the day it was needed — with the agency scope, the endpoints, and the limits set out plainly. When the first retest stumbled on a wrong agency slug in our own request path, the issuance on record is what the correction was checked against. A direct thank-you has already gone to Dante' from us; this is the public one. Thank you, Dante'. The regional map is whole again in part because a support engineer did his work well and quickly, and that deserves to be said where everyone can read it. The last dark layer The honest remainder, and the reason this edition waited to publish: DDOT's live vehicles. DDOT positions went dark on October 15 when the key hit its daily cap, and they stayed dark while SMART returned — a regional map with a dark home agency is a return with an asterisk, and we were not going to print "triumphant" over it. The asterisk is gone. DDOT live positions returned early on Friday, October 16 — in the first build cycles after midnight, when the BusTime daily transaction limit reset — and at the restoration verification the feed carried 33 DDOT buses alongside 93 SMART vehicles and the QLINE's streetcar: 127 live vehicles on the map. What remains open sits with DDOT, and it is the only open item left: the request to raise the key's daily cap to 50,000 transactions per day, with 25,000 stated as acceptable, sent on October 15. No decision had been recorded when this edition was finalized; the checkpoint stands on October 22. The daily reset restored service without the raise — the rebuilt feed runs at roughly 2,040 transactions a day against the key's default cap of 10,000 a day, inside the limit that reset at midnight. The request is about headroom, not survival — and the distinction is the whole story of October 15. The QLINE, for the record, never went dark. Its feed never depended on the shut-down host or the DDOT key, and it carried 4 streetcars, live, throughout — the interim this morning's edition described, now over. The close This morning's edition retired a public API and recorded an arrangement that did not hold. This edition records the arrangement that replaced it: licensed data, terms published before the feature returned, a draw of 1.7 percent of the issued limit, a display-only separation proven in the data itself, and a production state verified the same night by audit. The map is regional again — 83 routes, 10,583 stops, three agencies, live on infrastructure the Academy runs itself. The next arrangement was announced when it existed. It exists. Campaign-finance initiative (utilities and government contractors) An initiated law on the November ballot (official designation: Michigan Utility and Government Contractor Campaign Finance Regulations Initiative). It would prohibit regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to them from making campaign contributions to officeholders who impact them, and expand donor-disclosure rules for political communications. Signatures certified July 2026; ballot language approved August 2026. Southeast Michigan Public Historical Museum Authority millage (Wayne & Oakland counties) A 0.2-mill property tax (20 cents per $1,000 of taxable value) for ten years, 2026 through 2035. About $30 per year on a home with a $300,000 market value. Estimated 2026 collections, per the official ballot text published by the county clerks: about $17,733,800 in Oakland County and about $12,219,200 in Wayne County. The Authority's Articles of Incorporation — adopted by both county commissions in July 2026 — lock in the revenue split: 15% of each county's collections, after Authority administrative expenses, goes to that county for other public historical museums there (though either county may redirect its share to the two main museums); of the remainder, 60% to the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History and 40% to the Detroit Historical Museum and Dossin Great Lakes Museum. No millage revenue may pay for maintenance deferred before the Articles were adopted. The Authority must meet under the Open Meetings Act, comply with FOIA, and obtain an annual audit under government auditing standards; its museum contracts must include free general admission for county residents, free tours, programming and transportation for schools and seniors, and teacher curriculum support. If voters in either county reject the millage, the Authority dissolves. Official ballot question (Wayne County wording; Oakland County identical except county name and revenue figure): “Shall a 0.2 mill tax on all taxable property located within Wayne County be imposed by the Authority for a period of ten (10) years, being years 2026 through 2035, inclusive, to provide historical museum services for the benefit of the residents of the Counties?” Supporters say The campaign, Yes to Our Story (a ballot question committee registered with the Wayne County Clerk, funded by the two museums), says the millage delivers ten years of stable funding, free access for residents, students, and seniors, and support for dozens of smaller local history museums. Note: the Authority's adopted Articles now bind it to the Open Meetings Act, FOIA, and annual government-standard audits.
